This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable. A clear, step-by-step demonstration of this property is provided for zinbiel algebras defined by their multiplication table, followed by a broader discussion that explores the connection with another algebraic structure - the Malcev algebras - and demonstrates how a zinbiel algebra's properties can be determined from its fundamental identities. Moreover, the paper also delves into the relationship between these results and the renowned Poincaré-Birkhoff-Witt theorem. Lastly, it is demonstrated that the property of nilpotency is hereditary, meaning it is inherited by any quotient algebra of a zinbiel algebra. The paper concludes by examining the implications of these findings for the coefficients in a zinbiel algebra's universal enveloping algebra. The appendices provide additional information on the hereditary nature of the nilpotency property and offer a relevant counterexample, as well as a translation of the main results into the language of differential operators. The paper also acknowledges the contribution of an anonymous referee whose meticulous review included the discovery of a previously overlooked proof for a key statement and the suggestion to examine the connection with the Poincaré-Birkhoff-Witt theorem. The paper ends by highlighting the importance of this result in the broader context of the research on the universal enveloping algebras. This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, they highlight unique sensitivities to two crucial factors: the viscosity of quark--gluon plasma and the characteristics of the collisions' initial state. Given that these fluctuations tend to increase with the momentum of the particles, there is a need for re-examining existing theoretical models to gain a more precise and unbiased understanding of quark--gluon plasma's properties.

This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. Moreover, our work incorporates an original algorithm for data validation, along with a prototype implementation called InconTab, and we present InconTab's outcomes for both synthetic and real-world datasets. These experiments demonstrate that our approach yields a superior performance compared to traditional repair techniques. Finally, we outline possible directions for extending the InconTab system, including support for null-free data tables and cyclic functional dependencies. All implementation details, datasets, and performance evaluation metrics are available online at \url{https://github.com/alvin ewen/InconTab}.

This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. Our analysis shows that the time-varying parameters model generally outperforms its constant-parameter counterpart in terms of forecasting accuracy, as evidenced by both simulation and real-world data findings. The TV-PARX model's effectiveness is also reflected in the clear, interpretable results obtained from the analysis of these data sets. The introduction of the time-varying specification allows for a more nuanced understanding of data sets characterized by complex dynamics and shifts, further enriching the field of dynamic econometric analysis. The R package TVPARX, accompanying this research, enables users to implement the time-varying Parametric AutoRegressive with external covariates model in their own work. The package is freely accessible on CRAN. The research discussed herein is a part of the broader project examining the time-varying parameters model with the aim of discovering how the model's performance is affected by different state space specification variants. The results of these investigations are presented in the working paper titled "Time-Varying Parametric AutoRegressive Models: A Comparative Analysis" available on arXiv. The research was partially funded by the grant number 2020354 from the National Science Foundation. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classic scenarios. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty. These updated results confirm that the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity scales with the specific heat ratio as expected from conformal perturbation theory. Additionally, we have examined the universal exponent $\gamma$ and found it to be 1.412, 1.396 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Moreover, we have investigated the edge singularity's location and characteristics for $N=1$ and $N \geq 5$, finding that these cases differ from the classic universality classes in $N=2, 4$. For $N=1$, the Yang-Lee edge singularity is replaced by a second-order transition, whereas for $N \geq 5$, the universality classes become asymptotically mean-field-like. For these latter cases, we have identified the critical exponents and scaling ratios for the edge singularity. The most relevant classic universality classes in $N=2, 4$ are identified as requiring $N \geq 2$ due to the inevitable formation of a degenerate vacuum in massless $\phi^4$ theory. Consequently, we have found that the edge singularity's location and characteristics for $N=4$ are indistinguishable from those of $N=2$. The systematic uncertainty associated with the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for $N=4$ is driven by the assumption that $N$ can be less than 3.5, which yields a systematic error of approximately 0.5% in $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$. This is significantly smaller than the uncertainty associated with the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for $N=2$ due to the larger impact of the next-to-leading FDR correction term for $N=2$.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, initial pose regression or image encoding is performed to obtain intermediate cues, followed by a second stage of refinement. DeepHMap++, an enhanced version of the previously proposed DeepHMap framework, falls into the direct methods category where projections from a modern Auto-Encoder based object representation are used as input. In the proposed approach, a multi-scale projection group is created to cover the entire image by projecting the object onto different planes using different viewing angles. The projection groups are arranged in a pyramid structure, facilitating efficient feature extraction across various scales. A robust correspondence learning module is then employed to establish correspondence between the projected image and feature descriptors extracted from the pyramid. A novel projection group filtering mechanism is proposed to eliminate unnecessary projections, reducing computational expenses while maintaining performance. The proposed approach is evaluated on the BOP-2019 and COSE dataset, demonstrating superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at: https://github.com/zhengyang106/DeepHMap++.url}

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse formulations and notable
subcases like Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group, and Fused Graphical Lasso. The library utilizes SciPy for the optimization task and provides a user-friendly interface to tackle problems of medium scale. The framework is largely pseudocodes, making it straightforward to integrate custom optimization routines. The framework's versatility is demonstrated by the seamless integration of the Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group Graphical Lasso, and Fused Graphical Lasso formulations, all previously unaccounted for in available Python packages. The research highlights the significance of carefully evaluating the accuracy of configurational averages rather than relying solely on statistical fluctuations, in order to identify and rectify common pitfalls that can lead to flawed simulation results. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. A notable aspect of this study involves revealing the significance of pressures within the formed cavity in the surface-seal regime, which may have implications for broader applications in dynamics and fluid-related phenomena. This research involves a combination of both high-speed imaging and sensors measuring the pressure within the formed cavity, and includes discussions of the results in the context of existing knowledge on the subject. Moreover, we demonstrate that this particular D7-brane setup enables us to bypass the need for brane recombination, thereby offering a distinct and captivating perspective on the general principles governing Type IIB theories. This particular scenario where a spontaneously generated axion-like field arises from a broken translation symmetry in a compactified spacetime dimension serves as a notable example of this concept's applicability. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions. Furthermore, our results predict that the orbital selectivity and ferromagnetism could break down under strain or when substituted with another element, offering potential experimental verification of our findings. Moreover, we identify a range of low-dimensional quantum phases that could be accessed by applying pressure or chemical modification to the cubanite compound. Despite its complex chemistry, cubanite appears to have a simple and robust electronic structure, yet one that is highly sensitive to minor changes in its crystallographic arrangement. This makes it an enticing subject for in-depth theoretical analysis, as well as in-depth experimental study using techniques such as X-ray scattering, Mössbauer spectroscopy, and high-pressure experiments. The unique properties of this material could also have implications for our understanding of orbital selectivity in larger clusters, and make it a valuable compound for studying. A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. Notably, this breakthrough facilitates the creation of dark states within a short time frame, followed by the emission of N-phonon bundles, a novel multi-phonon phenomenon that can be influenced by an external magnetic field, but also occurs in its absence, thereby which allows for the generation of coherent acoustic bundles with N-phonons in just one round trip through the system. The model predicts that in a system with a dark exciton energy of about 1.8 THz, and after creating a dark state, and once the drive frequency matches the frequency of a sub-harmonic, the system will start emitting bundles of 6-phonons, a phenomenon that cannot be explained by a two-level quantum dot model. The novel feature of this system also enables the reliable production of acoustic solitons, another novel phenomenon that can be generated with a two-level quantum dot, but not with a more complex multi-level quantum dot. The theoretical predictions outlined in this study are supported by an accompanying experimental demonstration, which shows the production of giant dark states, followed by the emission of 6-phonon bundles, a phenomenon that cannot be explained by a two-level quantum dot model. The proposed system has the potential to provide precise control over acoustic bundles, as well as the generation of acoustic solitons, offered by the unique properties of dark excitons. The findings presented in this study contribute to the advancement of quantum acoustic resonators in metrology and communication systems, and offer new possibilities for the utilization of dark excitons in quantum physics. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. We also investigate the relationship between the distribution of photons and the detection of coherent states, revealing that the distribution of photons can be manipulated to enhance the quantum properties of SPCCSs. Furthermore, we propose an experimentally feasible design for generating SPCCSs using linear optics and parametric amplifiers, accompanied by a discussion of its limitations and potential improvements. This proposal offers a viable path for experimentally investigating SPCCSs and associated quantum phenomena using integrated photonic circuits and optical parametric amplifiers.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. This process is illustrated using both direct and indirect methods. Finally, we provide a concise overview of the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor and the related Stokes operator, followed by a discussion on their significance and relationship to the complex coefficients of the Riemann tensor. This review is intended for undergraduate students who have a basic understanding of General Relativity and electromagnetism within the Newman-Penrose formalism. It offers a step-by-step guide to converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis, and it provides a simple and accessible introduction to the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor and the related Stokes operator. This review can serve as a foundation for further exploration of advanced General Relativity topics, such as the complex coefficients of the Ricci tensor, the Ricci scalar, and the Einstein field equations, as well as the complex null tetrad basis in curved spacetime. It can also be used as a teaching tool for undergraduate students with a basic understanding of General Relativity and electromagnetism within the Newman-Penrose formalism. This review is composed of three main sections, each corresponding to a different method for converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. The first section explains the direct method of conversion, the second section discusses the indirect method of conversion, and the third section provides an in-depth analysis of the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor and the related Stokes operator. A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach excels in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also successfully modeling compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure. Furthermore, the method has revealed limitations in its current form, primarily related to the complexity of certain polymer topologies and the lack of descriptors for certain monomeric units. Developments have been shared in the appendix to guide future improvements, including new descriptors for ringed monomeric units and a technique for modeling more intricate polymer architectures. The code for the proposed method is publicly available, as is the dataset of predicted property values for polymers.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory constraints and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified by our prior work on a public code-mixing dataset and a sample protocol for hate speech detection. Ultimately, our goals are to stimulate code-mixing NLP research, foster collaboration, and attract funding to address real-world challenges facing multilingual societies.

Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, researchers have also determined that both the effects of local fields and spin-orbit interactions are vital to correctly determining the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers have used a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results of experiments, achieving a very accurate match. Ultimately, this research has clarified Ta$_2$O$_5$'s crystal structure, confirming the $\gamma$-phase as the ground state, and highlighting the significance of local fields and spin-orbit interactions in determining its energy loss.

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. Ultimately, our research revealed that The Big Sort's contribution to online misinformation dissemination exceeds that of other factors, suggesting that reducing demographic homogenization and promoting diversity and pluralism may be essential in reducing the spread of misinformation. The study's findings are relevant to the implementation of effective strategies for battling online misinformation. The underlying mechanisms and theories of this study's results can be applied to similar problems and phenomena beyond The Big Sort. The data used in this study may be useful for other researchers studying topics such as election interference, the spread of reliable medical information during the COVID-19 pandemic, or the circulation of vaccine misinformation. The findings of this study are also relevant to the ongoing debate about the role of fact-checking in reducing the dissemination of misinformation. The study's results suggest that fact-checking may be less effective in areas where residents are less diligent in nature. The study's findings about the relationship between demographic change and the circulation of news from high versus low-quality sources have implications for the understanding of social phenomena such as cultural evolution and provide a platform for studying similar phenomena in non-human primate groups. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. The findings presented in this research can be utilized to design more sophisticated learning systems for robots that incorporate spoken language during training. The study's results also provide insights that can be applied to human-robot interface development, informing the use of spoken commands to guide robotic behavior and correct errors. Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this difficulty is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in this context. A key unifying framework consists of Euler-Arnold equations and their broader integro-differential generalizations, ensuring the well-posedness of state or operator complexity optimization problems. Our comprehensive investigation extends upon our prior findings in arXiv:2005.02415, delving into intricate details of employed methodologies. A notable discussion involves differential regularization strategies, solving the integro-differential equation for Fubini-Study state complexity, and further exploring the underlying geometric properties. Additionally, we examine the generalized Euler-Arnold equations in both the discrete and continuous settings, concluding that they describe flat geometries. A connection to the natural metric defined by the Tracy-Widom structure function is established through the projection of these geometric surfaces. Our research introduces a key metric data cube, from which we derive important implications for state and operator complexity calculations. Moreover, we validate the energy-momentum tensor Gaussian state complexity calculations against numerical outcomes from quasi-exact density matrix evaluations, demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach. Our investigation highlights the fundamental role of geometric objects in determining the energy cost of state or operator complexity calculations in conformal field theories. Our research unfolds in the following sections: introductory remarks, a methodological discussion of our previous work, a review of the energy-cost data cube, a discussion of the underlying geometric properties, and a consideration of the energy-cost landscape in the discrete setting. Our findings provide a starting point for the exploration of non-Gaussian energy-momentum tensor states in 1+1 dimensional conformal field theories. Our research suggests that future studies could involve developing new numerical tools for the integro-differential Euler-Arnold equation, investigating the relationship between the energy-cost data cube and the underlying spacetime geometry, examining the impact of boundary terms on the integro-differential Euler-Arnold equation, and further analyzing the discrete landscape to extract fundamental geometric invariants. Our research delivers a significant advancement in the understanding of energy-momentum tensor complexity in 1+1 dimensional conformal field theories. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties of establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. This work was conducted as part of a larger project that also involves the development of a reasoning engine for conversational systems. This engine is capable of simulating the behavior of systems based on their knowledge graphs, and has been utilized in various applications such as fake news detection. This research was conducted within the Context of the Context Project. This paper is an abstract of a longer technical report that delves into the details of the proposed testing framework and an accompanying reasoning engine for conversational systems. This technical report and an accompanying system demonstration video are available online. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement Module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the preference weights for fusion. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Module to leverage the common, domain-agnostic aspect preferences for adaptation. MSDCR is evaluated on real-world datasets, and the results demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models in multiple settings. With its theoretical justification, comprehensive experimental verification, and code availability, MSDCR offers a valuable solution for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in real-world scenarios.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. These results highlight the complexities of generalizability in MRIQC settings and highlight the need for large-scale, integrated data analyses to establish universally applicable quality control standards. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Moreover, our research uncovers the key factors influencing the rendezvous process and reveals that this process can fluctuate between modes of successful meeting, modes of missed encounters and modes of sustained meeting. This paper's findings are accompanied by a supplementary video showcasing the agents' rendezvous dynamics over time. The proposed approach serves as a framework for other agent decision-making processes and offers a method for analyzing and visualizing their dynamics. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Additionally, we forecast that intermetallic compounds of the series could be synthesized and exhibit excellent mechanical strength due to their hexagonal closed-packed structure. Lastly, our findings suggest that all materials exhibit very low anisotropy and elastic strain, indicating their stability in various natural environments. Consequently, these materials have vast potential for use in three-dimensional networks, sheet, and bulk configurations.

The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that might be detectable with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator but are too heavy for the current LHC. Expected particle properties are listed in the paper, along with possible dark matter connections and suggestions for distinguishing the bilepton model from similar theories. Although the bilepton model cannot be confirmed through current data, predictions for the next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator are highly accurate, with a necessary collision energy of approximately 30 TeV for discovery. The paper also outlines three distinct scenarios for the bilepton model, each reflecting a varying degree of symmetry between the fermion and the gauge sector. The three scenarios - known as type A, type B, and type C - exhibit distinct predictions and could be distinguished from one another by studying the decay patterns of heavy mesons and baryons. The paper concludes by highlighting the bilepton model's potential to address open-ended problems in physics, such as the origin of dark matter and matter-antimatter asymmetry. Theoretical calculations for the paper involved using two different approaches to solve the renormalization group equations, with results showing that the predicted particles lie outside the current LHC detection range but could be found with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator. The predicted particle properties listed in the paper suggest that the bilepton model could be distinguished from similar theories like the $SU(3)\times SU(3)$ and $SU(4)\times SU(1)$ models, which predict different sets of heavy hadrons and may behave differently when studied at a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator. The paper finishes by emphasizing that the bilepton model is a comprehensive and self-consistent theory that can be confirmed or disproved with a next-generation 100 TeV particle

The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Moreover, we establish a connection between the standard ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, and the descent set of Bn. Additionally, our work includes the basis theorem as a special case, thereby generalizing the B-type Coxeter group basis theorem. Lastly, our results can be applied to determine the coefficient 1 of the Coxeter presentation for the finite classical Coxeter group Bn.

Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data.

The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Furthermore, we show that modulating the heat treatment duration allows for efficient coupling between the T center optical mode and a nearby microresonator, demonstrating that device design can be flexible and tailored to specific applications. The results presented here offer a foundation for advancing SOI T centers to be used in quantum communication systems. The findings suggest that heavy doping of the device layer, followed by a short heat treatment, will lead to high T center densities with favorable optical and spin properties. The distribution of the T center densities within the device layer can be precisely controlled by varying the ion implantation location. The short heat treatment required to enhance the optical emission of the T centers allows for the creation of high-density arrays of microresonator coupled T centers, enabling efficient coupling between the T center and the microresonator. The results presented here can be applied to a wide range of microphotonic devices, including waveguide coupled T centers, photodetectors, and quantum repeaters. The high levels of T center densities that can be achieved may also enable the creation of T center lasers and the incorporation of T centers into silicon photonic integrated circuits. The flexibility of the SOI T center system means that it can be adapted to meet the needs of a variety of quantum communication applications. of the context due to their extensive receptive field.

on the specific context in question. The evaluation method and context-aware
object detectors are demonstrated in a video for better understanding. The code
and data for this project are available at: https://github.com/achannarukul/Evaluating-Context-for-Deep-Object-Detectors.

We examine the concentration behavior of functionals of random vectors whose entries reside in the discrete cube. These vectors must adhere to the strong Rayleigh property, which is characterized by the condition that the total variation distance between the marginal distributions of a random vector and its permutation is bounded by a constant. We establish that the total variation distance between the distribution of a functional of a random vector and the distribution of the same functional evaluated at a fixed vector is also bounded by a constant. This result is further leveraged to demonstrate the subgaussianity of negatively dependent random variables, as well as strong concentration inequalities for random vectors with the strong Rayleigh property. Notably, we prove that functions of random permutations exhibit strong concentration inequalities. The discrete cube version of the Benjamini-Kalai conjecture would imply the subgaussianity of the number of isolated vertices in a random graph. The proposed approach yields a weaker bound on this measure, specifically that the moment of the nth power of the number of isolated vertices in a random graph on n vertices is bounded by a polynomial in n. Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Moreover, Springer demonstrated that the number of these conjugacy classes equals the number of conjugacy classes within the wreath product of the symmetric group Sn and the alternating group A_n, for n greater than two. Notably, this result can be viewed as a specialization of the Coxeter-Lexington conjecture, first proposed by the author. The original thesis titled "On symplectic transformations" is now expanded to include three additional chapters, covering crucial material and open problems in the field. The updated text also introduces a simpler, more direct proof of the mentioned Coxeter-Lexington conjecture. The updated thesis consists of six chapters. The first chapter provides an overview of the research, covering the basic definitions and essential background information. The second chapter explores the concept of recognizing classes of symplectic transformations. The third chapter investigates the structure of the symplectic group Sp_n(K). The fifth chapter delves into the specific case of Sp_n(Fq), a finite field with q elements. The sixth chapter offers some generalizations and considers the analogous problem for the symplectic group Sp_4(Fq). A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work is accompanied by a public repository containing the code and results for the experiments conducted. We also discuss potential avenues for unfolding the complex distributions of these models to unlock the full potential of NLP embeddings in various applications. Our research underlines the difficulties of unleashing the semantic capabilities of these models, as they are prone to capturing frequentist relationships rather than semantic ones. Our findings suggest that word2vec embeddings are essentially superficial, reflecting co-occurring patterns rather than inherent meanings, and that they are incapable of distinguishing between frequentist synonyms and opposing polarities. Our results demonstrate that these models are capturing temporal and spatial dependencies rather than semantic relationships. Our analysis highlights the challenges of separating the semantic and co-occurring distributions of these models, posing difficulties for various tasks and applications. Our research demonstrates that the word2vec model is a powerful tool for learning the complex structures of data but also emphasizes the difficulties of its interpretation, challenging many of its proposed uses. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This research is distinguished by its incorporation of both rationalizable and regret-free learning frameworks, contributing novel insights to the field of multiagent learning.

While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. Such a framework is presented here, facilitated by a command-line interface and customizable through configuration files, that can be utilized by groups with specific needs. The code, written in C, can directly utilize the APPL grid method for fast process evaluations and has been successfully employed in recent PDF fitting efforts. The framework's design allows for user-defined modifications to the underlying physics, giving rise to the possibility of extending it to related tasks beyond PDF fitting. The code is available upon request from the authors for the benefit of potential users. The framework's efficiency in evaluating physical processes is demonstrated, with a particular emphasis on the Drell-Yan process, relevant to LHC experiments, and the implications of PDF fitting bias are discussed. The code can be reconfigured to suit the needs of other research groups working on process evaluations and PDF fitting. The framework's design gives rise to the possibility of integrating new processes or PDF fitting algorithms with minimal effort, as exemplified by the inclusion of the xQTAG scheme in the code. The code has been applied to the evaluation of hadronic width in the $\rho$-meson, providing a previously unreported prediction, and giving rise to the possibility of extending it to the evaluation of hadronic decay widths in the heavy quark sector. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. The variance reduction based experience replay framework can be integrated into multiple policy optimization algorithms and is effective across a range of complex systems. The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/QiankunLi/VRBRR. The optimal policy discovery time is approximately 2 times faster, and the best policy found is generally 20% more accurate, as revealed by the experimental results presented. In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, particularly in highly 
branching scenarios. To evaluate the diversity of generated text, we introduce a 
simple scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, leveraging the 
expertise of our conversational dataset to assess the variety of generated 
text. Our research spans multiple text generation challenges on the MultiTalk 
Dataset, yielding surprising results as simple approaches often surpass state-of-
the-art deep learning techniques. Our findings are further validated through 
experiments on the automatically curated training data. Our dialog system, 
named DiversityExplorer, successfully produces diverse text across a range of 
metrics by exploring various branches of the MultiTalk Dataset. With its large 
scale and complex design, the MultiTalk Dataset offers opportunities for 
innovative tasks and metrics, paving the way for future research in the field.

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. The code is publicly available upon request. The accompanying catalogue encompasses 145 separate $f(R)$ gravity simulations, each with a distinct set of parameters, in addition to 5 reference simulations for $f(R)$, $f(G)$, and $CDM$ models. The data is accessible through the Centre de Donnees Cosmologiques (CDS) and the Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL) archives. The default implementation of the $f(R)$ gravity simulations employs the "logarithmic" form for the scalar function, namely $f(\phi) = \frac{\phi^2}{\xi \ln^2(\xi \phi^2 + 1)}$, where $\phi$ represents the rescaled curvature, and $\xi$ is a dimensionless parameter with a value of $10^{12}$ based on the current observational limitations. The recommended set of simulations includes mock galaxy distributions for the Euclid and the Square Kilometre Array surveys. The code's capabilities and the generated simulations are validated through a comparison with existing N-body simulations and observations of galaxy clusters and the cosmic microwave background. The results demonstrate MG-GLAM's effectiveness in producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and the code's suitability for creating large sets of simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy clusters and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We show that these domains are each tree-like in their interior and share the same boundary behavior, with the free field conditional on the boundary determined by harmonic extension from the boundary. This leads to multiple SLE with force being a special case of multiple SLE driven by stochastic log-gases. Ultimately, we establish that multiple SLE driven by the Gaussian free model on the line and the Gamma process on the positive reals exhibits the same behavior as multiple SLE with force, driving a domain that is the product of the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane. This in turn implies that multiple SLE with force is space-filling with a single connected domain as its limit state. This paper also introduces the concept of an imaginary surface evolving in time and associated Gaussian free fields, designating it as multiple SLE with branching, which drives multiple, space-filling, connected domains as its limit state. This model is capable of exhibiting various domain behaviors, from tree-like to full planar filling. This model's free field is again harmonic in each of its subdomains and shares the same boundary behavior as multiple SLE with force, but it exhibits different boundary behavior in its root domain than multiple SLE with force, driving a domain that is the product of the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane. Ultimately, this model allows for multiple SLE with force, multiple SLE driven by the Gaussian free model on the line and the Gamma process on the positive reals, and multiple SLE with branching as its special cases. This model's advantage over multiple SLE with force is that it enables driving a domain that is the product of any two subdomains of the complex plane. This model's disadvantage is that its limit state is determined by a parameter that lies outside of its natural time

MediaWiki's 'WorkingWiki' is an open-source extension that converts a wiki
site into a collaborative platform for developing papers and presentations
relevant to conferences and workshops. Based on the 'CopperBand' tool, which
automates paper and presentation formatting in line with ACM's guidelines,
WorkingWiki allows multiple users to work together on a variety of documents
including LaTeX papers, PowerPoint presentations, and HTML web pages. A
'Compile' feature is also provided to easily create PDFs from the wiki source
files. By integrating features of 'WikiLeaks' and 'CopperBand', WorkingWiki
facilitates seamless document development, review, and editing among research
teams using the MediaWiki platform. The project's source code is available
under the GNU General Public License v2.0 license. Visit the WorkingWiki
website at https://workingwiki.org/.

To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is shown to be challenging using existing models such as LES and DNS. Nevertheless, RANS models prove to be effective alternatives due to their ability to avoid closure issues. To apply these models, the researchers used LES to obtain the average flow conditions of the jet flame. Furthermore, the results from the model matched the outcomes from the LES simulations, confirming its effectiveness. An examination of the results from the model revealed that the time-shift of the reaction rate time-series data of the jet flame varies with different flow conditions, while the results from the model proved to be in agreement with previous studies conducted using LES simulations. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this work is to modify nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties, similar to the approach in nonlocal electrodynamics. The reformulated theory results in a constitutive relation identical to one proposed recently by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%. Additionally, we have identified key aspects of genomics that could underpin the large number of'mystery' associations and provide a framework with which to study new, newly discovered associations and traits. The associated data can be found at genomicurl.com.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered. These findings imply that discovering a specific source that remains inactive for a particular duration does not necessarily prove that the primary component is a black hole rather than a neutron star. Instead, such an argument would hold if it could be demonstrated that the majority of neutron star binaries have recurrence times shorter than a decade. For that purpose, future surveys are required to reveal the true distribution of neutron star binary outburst recurrence times within the Milky Way. Only then can we determine the size of the population of black hole candidates in the Milky Way, particularly within the center, by focusing on sources that remain inactive for a decade or more. If such a population exists, it could be confirmed by finding recovered outburst sources with similar spectra. If not, the majority of the Milky Way's neutron star binaries would have recurrence times exceeding a decade, and the theory that the long-quiescent X-ray binaries in the Galactic Center are black holes would gain significant support. If not, then the suggestion that the Galactic Center harbors a large population of black holes would remain unconfirmed. If the population of the Milky Way's neutron star binaries does extend to decades, then the predicted number of radio pulsars would also exceed the observed count, suggesting a larger pulsar population within the Milky Way. The estimated volume of the Milky Way's searchable volume for these sources would need to be recalculated based on the observed distribution of neutron star binary outburst recurrence times. If the searched volume for the pulsar population turns out to be larger than previously estimated, then the Milky Way's total pulsar population could exceed $10^{5}$. Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the NLI model's confidence achieves the highest performance to date. Secondly, this paper demonstrates a way to enhance the semantic variety of responses generated by the model through an iterative procedure called Diversity Threshold Generation, which, in comparison to standard generation methods, results in an average 137% improvement in NLI Diversity. The code for this research is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ParthGoi/ndp-diversity.

Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking. The results for the second scenario revealed the relationships between final mass and angular momentum, as well as the critical angular momentum required for mass shedding. This research also identified a unique relationship between the final objects and the initial objects, with objects that start as low-mass stars at high pressures ending their lives as low-luminosity cool objects. This led to the prediction that some very low-mass stars could end their lives as cool low-luminosity objects, rather than white dwarfs. The computer simulations were validated by comparing the results to observed data, particularly for brown dwarfs. The possible outcomes for these objects, with a range of initial masses and angular momentum, were simulated. The results suggested that even at very low masses, objects that start as low-mass stars with significant rotation could end their lives as cool objects, rather than white dwarfs. By incorporating this model, we obtain a range of afterglow phenomena and find that it successfully reconciles various previously distinct scenarios, including those during the initial highly relativistic phase, the transition phase, and the non-relativistic phase. This model also leads to the well-known $t^{-3/2}$ decay rate of afterglow signals in the non-relativistic phase. Furthermore, it predicts that there may be observable consequences of the initial highly relativistic phase, including the possibility of detecting high-frequency GeV-rays during the early stages of GRBs. This proposed model highlights the interconnection between afterglow phases and offers a unified framework for afterglow studies. It is noteworthy that this model was initially presented in arXiv:2105.02189 and arXiv:2105.02192. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. In order to enhance side-channel attacks, this research introduces a new technique, HyperDegrade, which incorporates previous methods and employs simultaneous multithreading architectures.  A novel analysis into the causes of performance degradation through cache eviction was also performed, leading to the discovery of an unknown source of slowdowns.  Compared to existing techniques, HyperDegrade resulted in more significant slowdowns and improvements, which in certain cases achieved an enhanced time granularity of three orders of magnitude for Flush+Reload attacks.  To further evaluate the technique, metrics for side-channel leakage were proposed, which demonstrated that HyperDegrade could be effective in side-channel amplification without compromising data integrity.  A fair comparison between three different performance degradation strategies in combination with Flush+Reload attacks revealed HyperDegrade's efficacy, which enabled the development of an attack on an OpenSSL vulnerability three times more efficient than other methods.  In addition, HyperDegrade's applicability to Raccoon-like attacks was also demonstrated, which can succeed with real-world data and extend the scope of existing attacks to various protocols, filling in the gap left by previous research.  The implementation of HyperDegrade is open-source and can be integrated into existing tools to enhance the efficiency of side-channel attacks.  A word of caution is necessary as HyperDegrade's design could potentially lead to a security vulnerability and as such requires hardware confirmation before its authenticity can be verified.
