A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by reaching small determinant values. This method was successfully tested on the 2D Hubbard model with a severe sign problem, resulting in accurate energy and spectral function calculations for finite temperatures and finite sizes. This complex network was also compared to its real-valued counterpart, demonstrating the benefits of using the complex version. The code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/AmritSarkar/Complex_Network_Sign_Problem. The signs' problem's influence on the network's performance was quantified in terms of the determinant's magnitude and its relationship to temperature, size, determinant masking, and fillings. The results show that this architecture efficiently mitigates the sign problem in Monte Carlo simulations. The code has been integrated into the ALF (Exact Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with Wave Functions) framework, a general-purpose toolkit for Monte Carlo simulations in quantum many-body physics. The framework, available on GitHub at https://github.com/ALF-Project/ALF, includes tools for resolving the sign problem and determining the optimal transformation for a given Hamiltonian. The complex network's performance was evaluated for a range of model Hamiltonians, including the 1D and 2D Hubbard models, the Heisenberg Hamiltonian, and the Hubbard Hamiltonian with next-nearest neighbor interactions. The challenge of resolving the sign problem in Monte Carlo simulations can be quantified in terms of the growth of the determinant's magnitude along imaginary directions in complex temperature planes. The 2D Hubbard model at finite temperatures and finite sizes with a severe sign problem is presented as a benchmark in this study. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both high-efficiency dense retrieval and a more effective pair-wise re-ranking process to produce outstanding results, surpassing non-retrieval methods and alternative baselines in our experiments. ReCross's versatility is demonstrated by successful applications in both within-dataset and cross-dataset evaluations. ReCross's source code is publicly available at https://github.com/THU-CLG/ReCross.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show that the duration required to achieve a desired level of privacy-Performance balance can range from a few hours to several days. The data also highlight the significance of limited batch sizing in extending the duration required to achieve the desired balance. The paper concludes by presenting an ongoing work that involves the development of a reinforcement learning-based solution to circumvent the challenge of limited batch sizing. The proposed solution, called PrivRL, leverages the results obtained from multiple trials to develop an enhanced policy that can be applied in various machine learning tasks beyond private deep learning. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection. Furthermore, we discover that the boolean complex of an n-node tree under the Weyl group generated by A_n has a homotopy equivalent structure to a collection of (n-1) spheres, providing a novel proof of a previously established fact by Bjorner and Weyman. For the finite groups treated in this study, we establish that their boolean complexes are contractible. Lastly, we establish an relationship between the boolean complexes of a group and its subgroups, giving rise to the notion of a boolean building. This leads to the introduction of boolean structures for the Weyl groups of classical Lie types, revealing that they possess a combinatorial interpretation akin to the root system itself.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning to capture implicit context relationships, which enhances the effectiveness of our models in forecasting peak and attenuation coefficients. To validate our approach, we applied it to real data and observed substantial improvements in forecasting accuracy. To illustrate the practical applications of this method, we conducted a case study involving the Beijing COVID-19 outbreak, demonstrating that our approach can effectively predict the peak and attenuation coefficients for a particular geographic region during a specific time period. To facilitate replication, we have made the code available online. This research contributes a novel approach to modeling the exponential distribution of online rumors and provides a practical solution for governing bodies to manage the spread of misinformation by targeting the peak and attenuation coefficients. This method can be applied to any data set, not limited to the Chinese context used in this study. To further enhance the effectiveness of this model, we suggest incorporating more advanced machine learning models, such as graph neural networks, that can account for the complex relationships between entities and their contributions to rumor propagation. This study provides a foundation for investigating other dynamic phenomena, including the spread of technologies, innovations, and policies, by analyzing the underlying exponential distributions. To facilitate future progress in this area, we recommend creating a research community focused on studying the distribution of adoption rates in social dynamics. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity of a particular spectral line, and velocity along the line of sight. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been applied using comprehensive planetary nebulae frequency distributions while also accounting for detection biases, and the resulting estimates of the distance to the Fornax cluster were calculated as 19.86 megaparsecs with an associated margin of error. Additionally, a significant agreement was observed between these new measurements and previously estimated distances using surface brightness fluctuations. The comprehensive nature of the planetary nebulae frequency distributions frequency distributions also enabled the calculation of the masses of bulge components within the galaxies, revealing a distinctive deviation from the typical galactic mass structure. The extensive nature of the data set and the analytical methods used are suitable for future large-scale galaxy surveys. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations. With its ease of programming and high performance, LifeStream opens up possibilities for medical researchers and clinicians to conduct complex, real-world data analyses. The system source code is available at \url{https://github.com/ StreamsGroup/LifeStream}.

A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space. Additionally, this research demonstrates that a specific type of curve, called the helical curve, is a special case of the newly defined category and satisfies the same properties as the original Bertrand curve in three-dimensional Euclidean space. Furthermore, it is observed that the (1,3)-Bertrand curve property can be repeatedly applied to any curve in a higher dimensional Euclidean space, defining a hierarchy of curve categories. A distinguished place within this hierarchy is found for the helical curve, designating it as a second-order Bertrand curve, and demonstrating how this property can be utilized to analyze the hierarchy of curve categories. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To demonstrate this insight's practical value, we develop a simple strategy for optimizing the choice of loss function and show that it can be effective in identifying desirable loss functions tailored to a particular dataset or task. Our research suggests that the community's unexamined assumption about loss functions may have limitations and that there's potential to discover more suitable ones, given the vast number of possible loss functions available. Our research is conducted using a broad category of neural network models, including residuals and graph-based models, and our findings are further validated on multiple public datasets. Our research's code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ghrua/Loss-Hopper. This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model utilizes a unique decomposition approach to the deformation gradient and applies the Coleman--Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle to material modeling. The resulting model includes suitable Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential assumptions, which enables simulation of crystalline region formation, degradation, and temperature changes during cyclic loading tests. Numerical implementation based on the finite element method provides the basis for numerical solutions, which include simulations of material sample microstructure and temperature evolution. This study's findings demonstrate that the proposed model effectively replicates the complex behavior of polymer crystallization during deformation and heating, offering a versatile tool with applicability to various polymer materials. The proposed method's advantages are also discussed, along with the research's potential extensions, such as incorporating orientation-dependent free energy and investigating shear-induced crystallization behavior. The model's code is available upon request.

Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis. Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification. This approach is useful for designing high-speed conventional differential detection systems. In particular, this research delves into the performance of CPM detection with $K$ symbol delays greater than one. For commonly used CPM formats, such as MSK, GMSK, and minisequence CPM, the results demonstrate how the optimal delay period can be determined once its characteristic polynomial is identified. This discovery enables the straightforward selection of delay periods even for CPM formats without a known connection to algebraic structures. In such cases, the desired performance can be achieved through delay period adjustment, facilitating design and testing tasks. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.  The comprehensive nature of ATOMIC also enables researchers to explore various aspects of machine learning-based commonsense reasoning and offers potential for developing sophisticated systems of artificial intelligence that can seamlessly integrate real-world data.  This dataset is suitable for developers of various deep learning models, including text generators and conversational systems.  Our accompanying benchmark, designed to evaluate the capacity of machine learning models for artificial reasoning across a diverse range of scenarios, incorporates nine diverse conditional inference tasks that require models to go beyond the limitations of isolated training data and demonstrate their ability to integrate real-world knowledge.  This has been confirmed by both objective performance metrics and subjective feedback from human testers.  We are making ATOMIC available to the public via our website.

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in an alternative space. This leads to speech representations being enriched with more linguistic information, while the text representations are made more similar to speech, enabling ASR models to effectively leverage unpaired text data for pretraining. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal a significant 6.15% reduction in word error rate when only paired data is used and up to 9.23% when additional unpaired text data is applied. This model also demonstrates its robustness in handling a wide range of hyperparameter settings. The code for this project is available at github.com/parikshitt/ multimodal_s2t.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. The conditioned random walk is analyzed to derive the desired asymptotic and limit results. The paper also includes an exploration of initially marked random parking distributions, demonstrating that the marked version of a distribution can affect its asymptotic behavior. The proof strategies employed here may be applied to other related models. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings. The complex nature of the nanowires may also be beneficial for implementing qubit systems. Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating the potential benefits of our proposed representation and future possibilities for its use in various applications. The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity. An examination of Anomalous Hall Resisitivity revealed that the Bismuth layers modify the Hall effect's scattering mechanism to the extrinsic skew-scattering type, suggesting that the spin-orbit proximity effect could result from elastic scattering of Cobalt's free carriers by Bismuth sites at the interface. This conclusion is further supported by calculations of Anomalous Hall Resisitivity based on the extrinsic skew-scattering type. The study of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers may open up possibilities for exploring non-abrupt interfaces' influence on Cobalt's magnetic anisotropy and also for generating the Rashba effect in this system. This could potentially lead to the stabilization of long-range ferromagnetism in Bismuth and may also provide a route to investigate interface-induced Rashba effect and its impact on the carrier distribution and the resulting magnetic and electrical transport properties in Cobalt/Bismuth and other semimetallic and superconductor systems. The research also suggests that the spin-orbit proximity effect and the resulting modified Hall effect and magnetic anisotropy may be controllable by adjusting the interface's scattering and the Cobalt layers' thickness. This finding offers a means to explore interface-induced modifications of Cobalt's and other ferromagnet's magnetic and electrical transport properties and could provide a basis for developing novel superconductor and semimetallic devices that rely on the spin-orbit proximity effect and the Rashba interaction. The study presents an explicit expression for the Anomalous Hall Resisitivity and offers a possible route to explore the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect, the Rashba interaction and its impact on the carrier distribution and the resulting magnetic and electrical transport properties in Cobalt/B

This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space variable $r$. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential becomes the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, solutions are obtained and expressed in terms of the Mittag-Leffler function and a fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function. Verification of the results is achieved by comparison with existing works, particularly for $\alpha=1$. Numerical examples, including a diatomic molecule, demonstrate energy eigenvalue and bound state eigenfunction calculations. The proposed model's applicability to scattering states and ground state energy for a harmonic oscillator with fractional uncertainty is also demonstrated. The generalised Mie-type potential's solution for $\alpha=1$ shows that the results coincide with those obtained using other fractional derivative approaches. The paper's mathematical framework is completed by providing a fractional derivative operator correspondence table. The results presented in this paper suggest that the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach offers a feasible and effective means of analysing the energy spectra of physical systems involving power law long-range potentials. The approach's utility in modelling real systems is illustrated by applying it to the hyperbolic potential, a well-known exactly solvable problem, and demonstrating the emergence of the scattering and bound states' characteristic spectra in the limit as $\alpha$ approaches 1. The paper concludes by highlighting the approach's potential advantages over other methods of analyzing similar problems. The results obtained for the generalised Mie-type potential, including the hyperbolic potential, are physically interpretable and provide a new insight into the long-range dipole-dipole interaction in the context of a diatomic molecule. The paper suggests that the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach's effectiveness in solving the time-independent Schrödinger equation for the generalised Mie-type potential, particularly in the limit as $\alpha$ approaches 1, offers a new means of investigating the energy spectra of power law long-range interacting physical and chemical systems. The results obtained for the hyperbolic potential, with its known exact solution, serve as a validation of the proposed approach and provide a new understanding of the long-range dipole-dipole interaction in the context of a diatomic molecule.

In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. The proposed method is comparable to alternative methods of regularisation but offers the additional benefit of ensuring the smoothness of the trained model, which is beneficial when deploying models in sequential applications. The code for our experiments is publicly accessible online. The proposed method is designed to work with existing neural network architectures, and we showed this by incorporating it into a pre-trained ResNet, which produced a working LipNet. We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. The code is made available through a public website. The simulations reveal that the constraints on vector leptoquarks with a mass of less than 870 GeV, which interact strongly with tau particles and electrons or muons, are more stringent than previously known, based on searches for similar exotic particles. The code can be used to further explore these constraints and investigate similar limits on vector leptoquarks that interact with other lepton pairs. The development of this code provides a useful framework for simulating other processes involving vector leptoquarks and ditau systems, given its efficiency and the accuracy of its corrections. The code can be used to generate events for searches of exotic particles at the LHC, as well as for studies of ditau systems in other contexts, such as quantum physics beyond the standard model. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these challenges. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans without corresponding MRI data to generate higher-quality PET images at standard doses. We further enhanced the framework's robustness to out-of-distribution data by introducing a robust overparameterized model to handle data perturbations. Experimental results on low-dose PET data showed that our proposed method outperforms existing baselines with lowered dose levels and data without corresponding MRI, demonstrating its versatility and versatility. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/Jin-wei-Tung/Tau-Net-UD.

A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Furthermore, the study finds that these computer systems already incorporate the coherence information required to recognize connections within the text, making CT's contribution limited. Additionally, the study discusses aspects that influence connections within the text but are not accounted for by CT, including the systems' knowledge and their tendency to favor more recent statements. By incorporating these elements, the study presents a revised version of CT and shows that it better captures the connections within the text compared to the original CT. The study's findings are supported by multiple experiments, including a interesting analysis of connections within the text in relation to a variable called "episode length". The study's conclusions are centered on the context of computer systems that identify connections within the text and cannot be directly applied to similar systems that generate the text. Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful data features from a set of conventional signal distance metrics using feature selection and genetic algorithms. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, models were tested on previously unused datasets from the training and validation stages. Furthermore, a comparative analysis was conducted among different machine learning algorithms utilizing a wide range of evaluation metrics, including their scalability to accommodate diverse real-world datasets. The findings of this research are significant as they provide a framework and guidelines for developing a wide range of distance estimation models suitable for a broad spectrum of indoor environments. The proposed approach is adaptable to new, untrained datasets and offers suggestions for further improving the model's performance. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. Furthermore, considerations for 6-D beam stability and hollow beam filling patterns are also discussed. This study highlights the significance of early design stages where filling patterns can be determined in conjunction with beam breakup instability control, beam dynamics, and RF system design. This way, optimal designs with minimal performance loss can be identified. This research was conducted as part of the US Department of Energy's Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E) TRANSCEND program.

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under the NMRK limit, this two-gluon CEV simplifies to a one-loop CEV for two gluons in N=4 SYM theory. Given its predicted form, this result can be compared with analogous findings from recent studies, notably those obtained using unitarity methods for all helicity configurations and in all kinematic limits. The one-loop two-gluon CEV in N=4 SYM theory is further analysed to identify remnants of collinear cones within six-gluon amplitude configurations. A hypothetical relationship between this two-gluon CEV and a specific six-gluon amplitude configuration can be tested under both low and high rapidity limits. The one-loop two-gluon CEV in N=4 SYM theory is also compared with its next-to-leading order counterpart, revealing both similarity and distinction, as well as providing a new interpretation of the six-gluon amplitude configuration known as the two-loop six-gluon amplitude in QCD. The results presented in this work demonstrate the one-loop two-gluon CEV in N=4 SYM theory for all helicity configurations and in all kinematic limits, thereby paving the way for its use in extending the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy in QCD. The one-loop two-gluon CEV in N=4 SYM theory is made available through an accompanying dataset. Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. Moreover, our findings highlight the fundamental concept that surface curvature necessarily gives rise to an end exclusion zone, further enriching the behavior of surface-grafted polymers. The theoretical framework presented herein serves as a valuable tool for investigating brush geometries on curved surfaces of any degree of complexity. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. It turns out that capping distances makes graphs that are hard to identify easily detectable. Next we discuss the relationship between two approaches: one based on the size of the largest cluster in the graph and the other based on the number of those clusters. Finally we examine the effect of capping distances on some specific graphs and the impact of it on the metric dimension of those graphs. Generally speaking, our research reveals the complex nature of the metric dimension parameterized by k. Here we outline a simple algorithm to determine beta_k of a given graph and use that to examine the behavior of beta_k for three example graphs: a circle, a torus and a hypercube. Surprisingly, our findings show that the metric dimension of these graphs increases dramatically as the distance between points is allowed to grow, ultimately becoming equal to the number of vertices in the graph. This behavior is unlike what happens with the same graphs where the largest cluster rather than the number of clusters is considered. In that case the metric dimension remains constant and equal to the number of vertices in the graph. This difference in behavior highlights the distinct effects of these two approaches and confirms that the metric dimension of graphs with many small clusters that are easily identified does not necessarily remain small. This is further reinforced by our result that detects a graph with an arbitrary large number of vertices with a certain property and shows that there are graphs with a specific property of finite metric dimension. This property is defined by the number of vertices in the graph and the distance between those vertices. This finding is significant because it resolves a problem posed by the first author and Guerra in 2014 and answers a question posed by the first author in 2020. This result is also relevant to a broader problem posed by the first author in 2020 about the growth of the metric dimension of graphs with a particular property. This result demonstrates that the metric dimension of a graph with a certain structure, in this case a specific type of clique-based structure, grows exponentially with the number of vertices in the graph. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. This study's data and algorithms are available for public use.

Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a $d$-dictatorship framework, which encompasses not only the celebrated serial dictatorship method but also other established problems such as multi-agent assignment tasks. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that a broad class of optimization problems, including some notoriously difficult problems like the $k$-facility location problem, can be efficiently solved using the $d$-dictatorship framework. We also provide a meta-algorithm that yields a approximately 61%-approximate $d$-dictatorship algorithm for a wide range of optimization problems. Moreover, our research shows that there are instances of the classic multi-unit assignment problem for which even the 2-dictatorship yields a significantly poorer outcome than does the optimal solution. Thus, our research highlights the importance of developing more sophisticated and problem-specific approaches for addressing the optimization challenges associated with the combinatorial multi-agent scenario. We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby stars. 
These methods yielded a set of candidate wide binary asteroids awaiting further
investigation with additional data, particularly from light curves and orbital
layouts. Our open-source code is titled `baa` (Binary Asteroid Analyzer). For 
each detected asteroid, our results are presented, incorporating their PSF 
features, orbital parameters, light curve periods, and predicted semimajor 
axes lengths. Our current findings consist of 14 certain and 37 possible wide 
binary asteroids within the main belt. Our discoveries particularly highlight 
the C-type asteroid (704) Olgaea, presenting both a long period light curve and
a predicted semimajor axis length of approximately 3 times its primary component's
Hill radius. Our code, research data, and findings are available at https://baa.readthedocs.io/. https://github.com/astropy/astropy-extensions/tree/develop/astropy\_baa. https://osf.io/5x8yd/.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Our findings are accompanied by a publicly available code and data, paving the way for future explorations in guided conversations. Moreover, we outline potential applications for the G4C challenge in areas such as education and customer service. The underlying data and framework are publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/nyu DAL}.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research suggests that the formation of knots in proteins could serve a significant purpose, offering a potential beneficial effect on their three-dimensional structure and stability. However, the underlying mechanism of their formation remains poorly understood. This study introduces a novel approach that leverages advanced topological analysis to identify specific folding pathways for proteins with trefoil knots, revealing that these pathways often originate from distinct conformational states and that the knots themselves can influence the proteins' conformational stability. Moreover, our findings demonstrate that proteins with trefoil knots typically form knots through a complex process involving multiple intermediates, rather than a simpler process called intramolecular slip, although the occurrence of intramolecular slip is more common for proteins with untied knots. Our results also show that proteins with trefoil knots exhibit a stronger preference for conformational states that facilitate knot formation over those that don't, and this preference can be exploited to distinguish between knotted and untied versions of the same protein using advanced spectroscopic techniques. This study's insights into the formation of protein knots were gained by examining a specific type of knot, but its analytical framework is general and can be applied to the study of other types of knots and protein structures. This approach combines machine learning, physical modeling, and advanced experimental techniques to provide a comprehensive understanding of protein knots and offers a potential means of designing novel proteins with desired structural properties. This research was conducted using a computational model and experimental data obtained through NMR and NMR-based hydrogen exchange experiments. This study involves a simulation of 50 trefoil knotted proteins, each with a unique sequence, and a theoretical model of its folding pathway, trefoil knot formation mechanism, and the physical basis of its conformation and stability, in addition to a physical analysis of its sequence, binding affinity, and thermal stability. This research demonstrates the benefits of considering the topological properties of proteins and provides a framework for studying other complex protein structures. If $X$ is a blowup of the toric variety $X_{\Delta}$ with a non-singular toric manifold $X_{\Delta}$ of dimension $4$, then we establish the relationship between the symplectic mapping class group of the pair $(X,\Sigma)$ and the symplectic mapping class group of the pair $(X_{\Delta},\Sigma_{\Delta})$, where $\Sigma_{\Delta}$ is any subset of $X_{\Delta}$ with an irrational property. Finally, we offer some concluding remarks and potential research directions.

Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. The code for this project is now publicly accessible at github.com/google-research/disco.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.  The paper also introduces a novel benchmark called Single2Multi, which consists of multi-image datasets alongside their single positive label data and corresponding ground truth multi-label data.  This new challenge is designed to evaluate the performance of models trained using the single positive scenario.  The results show that models trained on single positive labels excel in comparison to those trained on comprehensive datasets but struggle when the number of conditions to control for increases.  The datasets and an implementation of the proposed technique are available for use at https://github.com/zwang0329/single2multi.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms. From this perspective, consider the example of the algebra of compact operators, which yields a state representation corresponding to the Hilbert space of square-integrable functions across the unit circle. In this case, the relationship between the algebra and state representation 'forgets' the specific geometric characteristics of the circle, retaining only the circle's topological properties as defined by compactness. This perspective on the GNS construction encourages an interpretation of the abstract algebra as being intrinsically connected to the geometric properties of the classical world. This connection is particularly evident when considering the algebra associated with the M\"obius ring diagram, which generates the compact operators on a infinite-dimensional Hilbert space. This result provides a novel insight into the nature of the algebra as being fundamentally linked to the geometric properties of spacetime. This connection is further solidified when considering the projection operator GNS representations, which yield the projection operators corresponding to the state's support. These projections behave as idempotents that partition the system's Hilbert space into subspaces, providing a physical interpretation for the fundamental properties of spacetime. This formulation of the relationship between the algebra and state representation encourages an an analysis of the physical properties of the system being described, which in the case of the M\"obius ring diagram reveals the existence of a conformal group, specifically the $SO(2,2)$ group, that governs the system's spacetime properties. This result demonstrates the capability of the abstract algebra to capture the fundamental geometric properties of the system's spacetime. The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that there must be a weak gamma-ray signal or an alternative source of radiation.  Finally, in all cases studied, the energy of the gamma-rays remained below the expected level when comparing observations to the MAD model's predictions, indicating that the model, while intriguing, requires further development to fully capture the insurance behind the gamma-rays in these galaxies.  Nevertheless, the MAD model remains a promising theory that could account for gamma-rays in a wide range of environments, and its limitations offer valuable insights into the characteristics of the environments it seeks to explain.  Moreover, the finding that the MAD model works best for low accretion rates in galaxies with minimal cold gas also supports the view that the gamma-rays in some galaxies may result from the interaction between matter and the strong magnetic fields surrounding the black holes rather than the black holes themselves.  Finally, the MAG model highlights the significance of the interplay between charged and magnetic fields in environments where matter and magnetic fields are compressed and energized, leading to the formation of gamma-rays in galaxies, and its implications for the study of radiation in other environments.  The code for the MAD model is available online at [github.com/ysuryan/MDisk]. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes a Residual Neural Network (ResNet) and was tested on noisy recordings obtained from multiple stethoscopes, demonstrates a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing approaches.  The proposed technique achieves the best results across a wide range of recording conditions and environments, indicating its potential for low-cost implementation.  The findings provide a framework for creating cardiac auscultation systems capable of accurately diagnosing conditions even in noisy environments using low-cost devices.  The code for this study is available online at github.com/HeartSound/ResNet_FCN.  The optimal setup for the proposed method yielded an f-score of 0.78, a precision of 0.79, and a recall of 0.77 in the detection of systolic murmurs and an f-score of 0.69, a precision of 0.70, and a recall of 0.69 in the detection of diastolic murmurs.  The proposed technique effectively identifies cardiac auscultation sounds regardless of the level of additive noise or the degree of signal distortion, as shown in Figures 5-8. This study tackles a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly in time. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal cost function, as well as to demonstrate the existence of policies that minimize costs under this dynamic framework. Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001.
It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is to
determine the original transmitted sequence that corresponds to a particular decoded output.
It is essential to note that this problem differs from the problem of correcting errors,
as it is not necessary to recover the original transmitted sequence for all channels,
but rather to find the one that results in a specific decoded output.
The sequence reconstruction problem can be represented by a permutation matrix $\pi$
of size n x n, where the entry in the i-th row and j-th column, denoted as $\pi_{ij}$,
represents the number of errors between the i-th and j-th transmitted sequences.
The challenge is then to recover the original transmitted sequence from the permutation matrix $\pi$.
It is essential to mention that the sequence reconstruction problem initially arose in the context
of DNA sequence identification and has since found applications in channel coding theory,
group testing, and combinatorial optimization.
However, its connection to the mentioned areas remains largely exploratory.
The main contribution of this study becomes apparent in the final section, where we establish
the relationship between the sequence reconstruction problem and another problem known as dynamic
regular expression matching, and show that both problems can be solved using a specialized data structure
known as a binary try tree, by developing an algorithm that determines whether a string belongs to a language defined
by a regular expression in $\mathcal{O}(1)$ time, and another algorithm that reconstructs the original transmitted sequence
from a decoded output in $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n})$ time, where n is the number of states in the finite automaton. 
This study also investigates the problem of sequence reconstruction for the set of all permutations
by introducing a new approach that employs a particular distance measure known as the Hamming distance. 
The main difference of this approach from previous works is that it does not rely on the properties of the permutation group. 
The study shows that the sequence reconstruction problem for the set of all permutations with the Hamming distance
can be solved in $\mathcal{O}(n \log n)$ time, which implies that there exists an algorithm that, given a decoded output
of length n, reconstructs the original transmitted sequence

This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process. Moreover, we demonstrate that the exponential decay of a system initially arranged in discrete steps, with a second-class particle located at the origin, differs significantly from the TASEP speed process. The developed results also include proofs of the Bethe-Boltzmann distribution's convergence in TASEP with periodic boundary conditions and ASEP with periodic boundary conditions. The research utilizes the "TASEP speed process" findings and the ASEP system with a specific initial condition, where the system consists of two parts separated by a line that moves at a constant speed, not aligned with the x-axis. This approach enables us to analyze the probability distribution of the line's velocity and prove that it is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$. The developed results can be extended to prove the Bethe-Boltzmann distribution's convergence in systems with periodic boundary conditions. The key tool employed in the research is the "hydrodynamic" equation, which describes the ASEP system's asymptotic behavior. This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control. This study highlights five crucial aspects that offer practical value for researchers and healthcare professionals: the derivation of probability distributions for key epidemic indicators; the examination of a long-debated hypothesis related to the Kermack-McKendrick model; the analysis of critical time periods for model compartments; the identification of transmission threshold values; and the integration of model parameters into effective healthcare policies. By sharing these examples and results, we aim to inspire interdisciplinary collaboration that prioritizes the development of biologically informed models, rigorous assessment of their limitations, and a critical examination of research methods to better navigate the complexities of the ongoing pandemic and similar future epidemics. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. Furthermore, we explored two scenarios: one in which the dark state condition is met imperfectly, either generally known as the adiabatic case, or not at all. In the adiabatic case, we derived an inelastic non-rigid pendulum model, which enables discussion on magnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the emergence of large amplitude oscillations in magnetization. In the other case, we discussed the occurrence of magnetic death in a pendulum system without any deflection from the dark state condition. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. Our DNA-storage system is an open framework that can be utilized by various PCR-based data storage platforms. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of its proposed framework for predicting river flow velocities in changing environments. Additionally, we provide a Python code for the PCA-DNN model used in this study. Moreover, we offer a dataset of predicted flow velocities for the Savannah River over a 10-year period. This research can be extended to similar problems in the mechanics of continuous media by incorporating time-dependent solutions. Moreover, we propose a new quality metric, the ''flow velocity extrapolation error'', which can be employed to compare and validate models developed for similar problems. This approach can be applied to models such as the full Navier-Stokes equations, the Euler equations, and the Boussinesq equations, among others. This new quality metric can also be utilized as a basis for a new loss function, enabling supervised training of machine learning models developed for similar problems. Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. The authors open-source this framework for the research community to use, with potential applications in guiding related work sections and highlighting paper contributions. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation. The results show that the BDDC algorithm significantly outperforms the AMG method for solving the linear system in several relevant scenarios, offering a 5-fold reduction in solution time compared to the AMG method when solving a 13 million unknown system. A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically applied to a waveguide with a microresonator in close proximity, enabling the computation of mode coupling and phase modulation terms. Furthermore, a dimensionless equation is derived to describe the dynamics of two identical counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator and, under the condition of mode identity, it is proven that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation. The developed theory is expected to provide a versatile foundation for studying a wide range of phenomena in nonlinear and linear regimes. The code for the developed theory is available online at [1,2]. The findings related to a loop resonator may be relevant for nonlinear phenomena observed in systems such as Kerr microring resonators, as they often involve counterpropagating modes. The developed approach may also be applicable to other geometries, such as whisker resonators with a looped end, and it is hoped that it will facilitate progress in related areas. A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed turbulent velocity patterns from limited-resolution data across a range of Reynolds numbers. A specially designed multiscale model was utilized for high-resolution velocity reconstruction, with the assessment of its effectiveness being performed through direct numerical simulation data for turbulent flow with longitudinal obstacles at different Reynolds numbers. The evaluation showed that this deep learning framework accurately replicates high-resolution velocity patterns and statistical measures from two low-resolution data sets. Furthermore, it was observed that this model successfully recreates turbulent velocity patterns at Reynolds numbers that it was not originally trained on. The proposed method has the potential to enhance the resolution of real-world turbulent velocity patterns through a single training model. The proposed framework for turbulent flow and a related model for super-resolution image reconstruction share the same architecture, which is demonstrated to be effective in its respective field. The development of this approach provides a useful tool for conducting high-resolution turbulent velocity reconstruction from low-resolution measurements or simulated data. The code for this study is available at https://git.io/drivenet-turb. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this limitation, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. The framework and methodology are available open-source at https://github.com/nickbeine/L2Explorer.
