We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's total node count, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding a certain fraction of the genuine node count. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate based on node degree data collected during a preliminary protocol execution and subsequent post-processing of this data. Our theoretical analysis shows that the proposed algorithm yields a node count estimate that closely approximates the actual node count, with a margin of error bounded by a constant times the square root of the number of nodes multiplied by the fraction of malicious nodes. Moreover, the algorithm's implementation requirements for each node are minimal, with a limited memory footprint and a simple, efficient computation routine. Our evaluation of the algorithm on real-world datasets reveals that its efficiency is practicable for a wide range of network sizes and types, with a particular emphasis on the reliability of our implementation in environments compromised by malicious nodes. Our research also produces a lower bound on which any network size estimation algorithm would need to surpass in order to surpass the performance of our current algorithm. Our findings related to the algorithm's performance on real-world datasets are particularly notable because, to our knowledge, this is the first study to examine the scalability of network size estimation algorithms on modern datasets. Our research on the theoretical limits of network size estimation algorithms also produces a notable outcome: we demonstrate that, in general, any node count estimation algorithm would necessarily require a node population that includes a significant number of nodes with a degree of one in order to yield a accurate result, with a particular emphasis on the necessity for a dense enough population of one-degree nodes in the context of complex, small-world networks. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. Our research shows that this new approach offers significant improvements in solution accuracy and marked reductions in solution time when compared to the conventional multigrid solver for a broad range of representations, transforming it into a highly effective tool for solving the initial data constraints in numerical relativity. Our code is an extension of the Einstein-Cartan-Caucy code and the Conformal Transverse-Traceless Decomposition code. It is capable of generating quasi-minimal solutions and features improved performance for complex representations. Our research data are available for download at [www.doi.org/10.15480/2023.12.13]. Our code can be accessed via Git repository at [www.doi.org/10.15480/2023.12.14]. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. A comparative analysis with theoretical predictions from first-principles calculations and Boltzmann transport theory enables us to gain insights into the underlying electronic and magnetic structures influencing the anomalous Nernst effect in this material. Ultimately, this approach enables us to define an explicit function f_n(s) for each n > 0, consisting of integers, such that the set of integers n for which H_n is non-trivial is precisely the set of integers n such that f_n(s) is non-zero for all s < 1. Moreover, we offer a simple, verifiable formula to calculate f_n(s). This includes the special case where G_K is the absolute Galois group of the rational numbers, yielding a function f_n(s) equal to (n-1)*(n-2) when n > 2, (n-1) when n = 2, and 0 when n = 1, indicating that the set of ramified prime numbers for the rational numbers is precisely the set of prime numbers 1, 2, or 4 more than a square. Lastly, we offer a possible approach to extending this result to GL_n for any n.

Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations. 
The novel methodology presented has vast potential applications in evaluating the condition of composite structures in various industries including aerospace, marine, and sports equipment.

All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a heightened level of symmetry. Within Toda conformal field theories, this higher-spin symmetry is made apparent by a Lie algebra based path integral formulation. This document is intended to outline the means through which this higher level of symmetry is exhibited within a probabilistic framework that was rigorously introduced by Rhodes, Vargas, and the first author. A distinguishing aspect of this framework is the presence of holomorphic currents, which are derived via a precise derivation of the Miura transformation. Notably, we demonstrate that the spin-three Ward identities, which embody the principles of higher-spin symmetry, are applicable in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. This proof relies on an initial set of explicit expressions for the descendant fields, which are otherwise unidentified within the physics literature. This representation of descendant fields enables the derivation of the spin-three Ward identities through a transformation that exposes the underlying Lie algebra structure. This derivation serves as a significant extension of a prior, lesser-spin analysis performed by the authors in (Ann. Inst. Henri Poincar\'e Phys. Theor., 2020). We demonstrate that Coxeter groups possess biautomatic properties, resulting from which we derive that uniform lattices within isometry groups of buildings also exhibit biautomatic structures. This latter inclusion connects to the discovery that such lattices have a specific type of finiteness property known as Property R, initially established for geometric buildings by Swarztman and later extended to general buildings by Shwartzman and Drutiu. This work builds on the findings of Bestvina and Fujiwara regarding hyperbolic groups with a particular type of finiteness property. This biautomatic nature of Coxeter groups can be viewed as a variation of the established fact that these groups possess a system of polynomials. This new characteristic shares some analogies with the polynomial structure of Coxeter groups, as it results from the biautomatic property and encompasses distinct metrics that satisfy specific growth conditions, ultimately leading to the conclusion that these groups are rational, a property shared with hyperbolic groups possessing Property R. This work also includes an examination of the biautomatic nature of graph groups, leading to the discovery that these groups are both rational and have a system of polynomials, which distinguishes them from groups obtained through Higman's embedding procedure. Lastly, this research demonstrates that the biautomatic nature of a group $G$ is equivalent to the solvability of its presentation, as exhibited by the example of a heuristic Coxeter group, which is biautomatic but cannot be defined by a system of polynomials. Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. The results presented have important implications for the development of future BCIs designed to control more complex aspects of walking in individuals with spinal cord injuries. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond data classification, and providing insights into the underlying mechanisms and relationships among system components. Yet, most current techniques overlook this temporal aspect, making it a significant challenge to extract dynamic conditional connectivity matrices from time-series data. Here, we introduce a novel neural network framework, DCEN, that learns both the conditional and observed connectivity matrices from multivariate time series, and showcases DCEN's potential applications in neuroscience. Specifically, we use DCEN to estimate dynamic effective connectivity in fMRI data, and demonstrate its superior performance compared to existing methods. Moreover, DCEN enables the derivation of directed connectivity weights based on a generative model, which differs from many current graph-based neural network approaches. We also explore different DCEN variants and offer a practical guidance on model selection. Finally, we discuss DCEN's broader implications and potential uses in other domains. All code and data for this study are available online at this link: https://github.com/liyuchenDCEN.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation (SOR). In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called the 'Nested Neumann' Series, which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that this method converges at a rate determined by the eigenvalues of the matrix inverse. Moreover, we derive an explicit formula for the nested Neumann Series within a limited inception depth, demonstrating its equivalence to a higher-order matrix inversion. The proposed algorithms have been implemented in MATLAB and Cuda, and our results indicate that the 'Extended Nested Neumann' Series outperforms state-of-the-art methods including Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and SOR when dealing with large-scale sparse matrices on a Tesla V100 GPU. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Our method has been made available open source. Our study also highlights the importance of accurately modeling collision time steps. Our algorithm addresses this issue by providing a method of determining the appropriate time steps for simulating sediment transport. Our findings are expected to improve simulations of complex flows with numerous particles. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. This finding has significant implications for the development of control systems for legged robots moving on soft ground. This resulted in the robot demonstrating stable hopping behavior on softer terrains. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. The discovery's broader implications for quantum annealing algorithms and its potential to enhance problem-solving efficiency through data-driven analysis are discussed. The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present within compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star with density $\sim 4\rho_0$ exhibits gravitational acceleration within reach of current detectors, it's essential to investigate the possible indications of dense matter properties, such as the occurrence of strange quark matter. Although this scenario would require very advanced detectors in the near future, it's vital to explore theoretical models of dense matter, including strange quark matter.  In this research, we examine a specific model of strange quark matter, known as the "Nambu--Goldstone mode" scenario, which arises when the strange meson mode is excited and results in a very steep sound velocity versus density relationship.  By analyzing the characteristics of this matter model using hadron-quark hybrid QCD, we find that it could potentially give rise to compact stars with densities between 2 and 4 times nuclear saturation density, and examine the possible constraints on this model based on current neutron star radius measurements.  The prediction that this model makes about the occurrence of significant gravitational acceleration within the density range of 2-4 times nuclear saturation density, could be confirmed or refuted by future neutron star radius measurements.  This particular model matter can also be distinguished from other dense matter models, such as condensates of $K^0$-$\bar{K^0}$ pairs, which may also give rise to compact stars, although they would have different properties.  This research highlights the potential of future neutron star radius measurements in confirming the occurrence of this particular model of strange quark matter, which could give rise to compact stars with densities between 2 and 4 times nuclear saturation density.  If confirmed, this would open a new avenue for investigating the properties of this model matter through the analysis of future gravitational wave signals from compact stars. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. A particular pattern emerges where VSI primarily occurs in regions with a specific temperature profile, and particles' growth accelerates settlement-driven VSI suppression. Ultimately, our findings suggest that particles can exert a controlling influence over VSI, limiting its impact on dust evolution and settling behavior. This relationship between VSI, gas temperature, and particle growth may further refine our understanding of dust evolution and particle development in protoplanetary disk systems. This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional. Moreover, this finding has significant implications for solutions to a certain type of semilinear heat equation on these manifolds, where it ensures the finite-dimensional nature of the space of solutions that exhibit polynomial growth. Notably, this result superseds an earlier outcome for a particular type of manifold where the curvature is closely linked and allows for a key compactness result for a particular class of manifolds, ultimately leading to the proof of a conjecture regarding the lack of bounded harmonic sequences on a particular type of manifold where the curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant.

Recent advancements in outsourcing training and machine learning as a service have created innovative threats such as hidden functionalities that are embedded in artificial neural networks. In typical research scenarios, triggers that activate these embedded features are static in their positioning and pattern, thus enabling detection mechanisms to function effectively. However, researchers have recently discovered methods like Neural Cleanse and ABS to be vulnerable to triggers that are dynamic, meaning they are unaffected by pattern or location, thus compromising their reliability. What is even more challenging, is that these sophisticated backdoors require an inordinate amount of compromised training data. In a breakthrough study, it has been found that even without significantly compromising training data, hidden functionalities could arise from the presence of a single compromised sample, especially when the classification model employs a global average pooling layer. Furthermore, it has been discovered that overfitting plays a crucial role in creating these advanced backdoors, both dynamically and statically. Lastly, it has been demonstrated that both of these scenarios areenable to be circumvented through the intentional creation of models that are prone to overfitting, thus compromising the security of machine learning systems. This research uncovers novel and interesting aspects of hidden functionalities that have not been explored before, thus providing a significant amount of useful information for system security experts. This information includes but is not limited to the necessity of supervising models for overfitting, closely monitoring outsourcing training, and securely managing single sample training data. High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied the effects of varying $\gamma$ on parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Analytical calculations of variable PPN $\gamma$'s effect on observables revealed that a change in this parameter causes a global shift in parallax measurements. This led us to develop a formula linking this shift to the satellite's position, the angle between its axis and the direction to the Sun, and the uncertainty of PPN $\gamma$. Computational simulations validated our theoretical predictions. Given current $\gamma$ estimates, we believe its impact on the Gaia parallax measurement zero point is likely minimal, under 0.2 microarcseconds. Additionally, we found that this effect varies significantly with ecliptic latitude, primarily due to the Gaia scanning pattern's asymmetry, supported by additional simulations inverting the direction of the spin axis' precession. This Gaia lattice simulation reveals that the signature of this effect in the Gaia data should be identifiable, with a periodic pattern of parallax measurements fluctuating by up to 0.5 microarcseconds over a 6.5-year period. This prediction suggests a more constrained $\gamma$ value could be derived from future Gaia data, with implications for cosmological applications. This finding also highlights the importance of considering the satellite's position and direction in the Earth-Moon-Sun frame when analyzing parallax measurements. This research was conducted as part of the Gaia Inertial Reference System working group. A more comprehensive investigation into the PPN $\gamma$ uncertainty's effect on the Gaia catalog will be presented in a forthcoming paper. Given its relevance, this study's results may be applicable to similar astronomical measurement projects.

To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. Furthermore, an in-depth analysis of the results reveals that the approach's ability to handle questions relying on general world knowledge is particularly enhanced, with a significant improvement (12.3%) observed in such cases. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/ghru/CCQAKAA.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. The proposed method is further extended to handle node addition/dropout events, as well as random walk learning without connections between nodes. The efficacy of the proposed algorithm is demonstrated through random walk learning without connections between nodes, with both synthetic and real-world data. The code for the proposed algorithm is available at: https://github.com/AminGohar/random-walk-learning. The proposed algorithm has the potential to scale deep learning models to millions of nodes in the context of Federated Learning. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly for those with severe mental health disorders.  An examination of which types of treatment led to these results is complicated by inadequate data, yet indications are that both outpatient and inpatient treatment lower the odds of recidivism.  Mental health treatment appears to lower the odds of recidivism more quickly, with the reduction in odds peaking at three years, rather than further increasing at the six year mark examined.  A substantial decrease in repeat felony offenses among those aged 50 and older who had severe mental health disorders was observed.  Further research is needed into the specifics of treatment and the underlying mental health disorders, but the results suggest that court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation lowers the odds of future crimes.  The study utilizes a novel method of measuring mental health treatment and examines the potential effects of several confounding variables, including demographic changes, overall crime rate trends, changes in sentencing policies and guidelines, as well as the implementation of pretrial release programs.  The findings have implications for the efficient use of limited resources within the criminal justice system and suggest that funding mental health treatment may lower the long-term costs associated with recidivism.  The results also highlight the importance of integrating the social services and justice systems, which can provide continued access to mental health treatment for those who need it, in order to enhance public safety.  The study further recommends examining the specific types of treatment and underlying mental health disorders that lead to reduced recidivism rates in order to guide more effective use of resources, as well as investigating the generalizability of the results to other populations. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations of the proposed technique on brain and pancreas segmentation tasks using publicly available datasets show its superiority over current state-of-the-art methods. Code for the proposed method is available at https://github.com/linge-yu/CRSSS.

To gain a deeper understanding of the performance and lifespan of materials, 
it's crucial to assess their atomic disorder levels. To this end, we use a unique
approach that leverages graph neural networks to create an interpretable disorder 
metric, effectively capturing local atomic configuration variability across the
solid to liquid phase spectrum. This methodical approach is tested with three
models featuring different disorder levels, including interfaces between solid 
and liquid phases, multi-crystalline microstructures, and grain boundaries, 
using elemental aluminum as a prime example. Our study demonstrates how our 
approach tracks the space-time progression of interfaces and uncovers the unique 
topological signals of individual atoms, thereby enabling precise visualization
of the space-time progression of interfaces and the localization of defective 
sites within multi-crystalline structures. Furthermore, we evaluate the robustness
of our approach across various models and disorder levels, highlighting the 
potential of this framework to be applied across a broad and varied range of
materials and alloys. Our research is concluded by outlining promising future 
directions, including the integration of thermodynamics into our model, the 
investigation of stackings and slip systems, and the analysis of atomic defects
in layered materials. Our graph neural network based disorder metric is made 
publicly available at (https://github.com/material-gnn/disorder-meter).

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis. These applications involve estimating the expected number of mixtures in sampling problems and modeling genetic variation in yeast. The results suggest that GMLE's performance compares favorably to other methods used in these contexts. The appendix contains additional simulation results and details on the GMLE's asymptotic behavior. The R package called 'gmle' is available for implementing these methods. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. The finest results were obtained by employing a 4096-dimensional vector for the last fully connected layer, which led to a 12% reduction in word error rate compared to the baseline system. Moreover, incorporating the Czech training data led to a 5% error reduction, with a 5-fold increase in the required memory. We also investigated other parameters to optimize the system, including the learning rate, batch size, and frequency of label smoothing, and found the ideal values to be 0.0025 for the learning rate, 80 for the batch size, and 0.01 for the label smoothing, resulting in a 3% error reduction below the baseline system. The proposed system was then compared with a multilingual model, and although it exhibited a 7% error increase above the multilingual model, it showed a 5% error reduction compared to the standard baseline system. We also examined the effect of different data sampling strategies and found that the simplest uniform sampling yielded the best results. Finally, we tested the system on two dialects of the Czech language, namely the Prague and Central Czech, and obtained a 4% error reduction below the baseline system. The proposed system's simplicity and a 12% error reduction below the baseline system make it a suitable and high-performance transfer learning approach for Czech ASR. We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a static and spherically symmetric relativistic star comprising two fluids with anisotropic pressures, leading to the derivation of anisotropic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in covariant form. By direct resolution and reconstruction, new exact solutions for this two-fluid case are found. Additionally, three theorems applicable to the single-fluid scenario can be adapted to yield two-fluid solutions from their single-fluid counterparts. This approach allows for the generation of two-fluid solutions from known single-fluid solutions. Specifically, three new two-fluid solutions are derived from known single-fluid solutions, and two new solutions are obtained using two of the three mentioned reconstruction theorems. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain. With only 200 parallel sentences available for target domain training, our method achieved a relative improvement of 24% in the F-score over a standard multi-task training approach. Moreover, domain adaptation performance was evaluated using additional target domains and our method's sensitivity to hyperparameters, model complexity, and important factors for practical application. Our code has been made publicly accessible at github.com/salemtk/FewShotGEC.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose procedure for obtaining allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In the self-interested case, we discovered that for both of these methods, there exist mechanisms that result in equilibria that are fair allocations for all involved agents, using only their declared values as input. Nevertheless, we were unable to extend this success to allocations that are fair up to any good for more than two agents. In fact, we constructed a counterexample demonstrating that for agents with integer values, there cannot exist a mechanism that always produces pure Nash equilibria in the FFX relaxation for more than two agents. This serves as a significant limitation, as it shows that despite its appealing properties, the FFX relaxation does not generalize well to self-interested agents in situations with many participants. This discovery also highlights the importance of further investigation into the property of being envy-free for more than two agents. This research was initially presented at the 52nd Annual Conference of the Special Interest Group on Theory of Computer Science (STOC'20).

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  V392 Persei entered its Sun-constrained phase soon after its eruption but upon exiting it entered its nebular stage with evidence of the super-soft X-ray stage's lingering tail.  Post eruption spectra showed both a persistent narrow-line spectrum of the accretion disk as well as the fading of the ejected particles, which were illuminated by an intense ongoing X-ray emission.  Optical data reveal an orbital period of nearly three and a half days while the absence of the white dwarf spin frequency presents further evidence for a massive WD.  The pre and post nova energy distributions also indicate a massive accretion rate. The extensive optical and gamma-ray monitoring of V392 Persei, which is a first for a classical nova, as well as its unique persistent high state, make it an interesting target for future X-ray and gamma-ray observations, particularly after it went into its quiescent state in 2021. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Experimental results, using real-world FDD test data, demonstrate the efficacy of this GMM-based method. Furthermore, an analytical discussion on GMM-related parameters is provided, offering valuable insights for practicing engineers. The proposed technique's suitability for dynamic TDD systems is also explored, highlighting its potential to address key challenges in this context. The total data exchange between base station and mobile terminal is shown to be 5148 bits for a 20 MHz channel, presenting a significant reduction in overhead compared to traditional approaches. The codebook diversity gap is analyzed, leading to the recommendation of a specific GMM parameter configuration to minimize this effect. The impact of various GMM parameter settings on system performance is assessed through simulation, demonstrating the importance of proper configuration to maintain performance gains. The codebook construction process itself is optimized by developing a novel adaptive clustering algorithm, capable of efficiently constructing codebooks in scenarios with limited terminal memory. The effectiveness of this algorithm is validated through simulation, showing a 95% reduction in codebook size without compromising performance. The proposed GMM-based feedback encoding technique is further modified to create a hybrid approach, combining this method with the traditional quantity-based feedback scheme. The benefits of this hybrid technique are demonstrated through simulation, presenting performance gains of up to 12 dB in CQI estimation accuracy. The proposed GMM-based codebook and feedback encoding scheme, as well as the hybrid quantity-based feedback encoding technique, have been implemented in real-world FDD base stations, using actual data and infrastructure. The results show that the GMM-based codebook and feedback encoding scheme reduces overhead by 50% and improves system performance by 10 dB, respectively. The hybrid quantity-based feedback encoding technique delivers performance gains of up to 12 dB in CQI estimation accuracy. The proposed schemes are applicable to a range of scenarios, including dynamic TDD systems

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On conventional computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
To demonstrate its effectiveness, we saw fit to repeat and enhance previous studies' experiments utilizing this accelerated version of the text games. 
Consequently, TextWorldExpress becomes an advanced tool for evaluating virtual agents in text-based environments. The framework underlying TextWorldExpress is openly accessible via GitHub, enabling developers to create their own high-performance text games. Moreover, we are confident that its processing speed can be further improved to reach two billion actions per second on present-day hardware. 

Our research was supported by the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation program through the ROBERT project, under grant agreement number 828676. 
The affiliated codes and data for this research are available at https://textworldexpress.github.io/.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposed hardware model called TIE in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and energy efficiency in various benchmark tests. The designed FDHT-LSTM network also demonstrates high practical value, having been successfully applied in low-resolution video recognition scenarios. The proposed integrated design of the FDHT-LSTM algorithm and hardware, coupled with its practical applications, provides a significant breakthrough in the use of high-performance LSTMs for video recognition. The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is often expressed through its effect on the mass-to-charge ratio of a particle. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy, which must remain non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field theory, where a relationship involving the dimension of an operator exists and forms a convex function of the operator's charge under a U(1) symmetry. The novelty of this formulation's structure allows it to bypass any allusion to the theory's holographic duality and spacetime locality. Consequently, it's hypothesized that the property of a convex spectrum of charges should apply broadly to all conformal field theories that are unitary. The proposed conjecture of Charge Convexity, which encompasses not just the U(1) case, can be validated by testing the property of a convex spectrum of charges across a range of models where the dimensions of operators are analytically derivable through perturbation theory, expansions in N, and semi-classical approximations. Our exploratory examination reveals that the Charge Convexity Conjecture is upheld in each instance examined, yet we have not discerned the underlying reason for this behavior from the perspective of conformal field theory. The proposed conjecture of Charge Convexity holds particular significance for its potential to provide insight into the fundamental mechanisms governing conformal field theories within anti-de Sitter space. The Charge Convexity Conjecture can be formally stated as follows: The charge-dependent dimension operator is a convex function under the maximum norm, for all unitary conformal field theories in (1+1) dimensions. The property of Charge Convexity observed in the theory's perturbative, large-N, and semi-classical regimes suggests that it could potentially be a universally inherent property of all conformal field theories, especially unitary ones within anti-de Sitter space. The conjecture presented can be validated through analytical derivation of dimension operator expressions in various scenarios, offering a framework for which the property of Charge Convexity holds, and providing a possible starting point for further investigations into the underlying mechanisms governing conformal field theories within anti-de Sitter space. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings. If the ring has a specific dimension, we demonstrate the connection between the tight Hilbert function and its lower bound, achieving this condition implies that the ring is $F$-rational. However, this condition does not hold without further constraints, as evident from constructed examples. The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, there are significant performance gains to be had, particularly when comparing the results with those from continuous markets. Additionally, the introduction of a price response from agents in redispatch markets can lead to undesirable market scenarios, especially with large price swings. The model can be utilized to gain a deeper understanding of design options for ancillary services and electricity markets, and is available for download on GitHub. The development of the model also raises several research questions for the energy policy community. The model can be applied to real-world data, as demonstrated by the examination of a redispatch design issue in a German electricity market. The results showed that there are significant performance gains to be had from implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets. The model further revealed the causes of these performance gains and showed that the benefits arise from the effects of price swings on peak redispatch volumes and the reduction of imbalances. The model can be used to examine the performance of redispatch markets with order types in different settings, and is available for other researchers to use. The model consists of six clearing algorithms, and the results of its application suggest that the benefits of order types are greatest when there are large price swings and multiple producers with access to the same generation unit. R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-fold) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the polynomial equivalent of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the Chowla's conjecture regarding autocorrelation, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields. In addition, it provides an analysis of the prime factorization of composite polynomials and their iterates, revealing the possible distribution of these primes according to the mth wreath product of the Galois group S_(nd) for n > 0. Moreover, it explores the connection between prime factors and the polynomial's composition, revealing the distinctive and invariant property of such systems. In the course of this investigation, it is necessary to introduce a novel concept called the polynomial's reduction group, which serves as a natural extension of the standard concept of the reduction group. It is also discovered that the property of being regular or irregular systems can be determined based on the composition of the polynomial and its mth iterate, providing an alternative proof of a previously established finding by Odoni. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the property of being a regular system is equivalent to the distribution of prime factors being uniformly distributed according to the mth wreath product of the Galois group S_(nd) for n > 0, which in the case of large finite fields leads to the distribution of prime factors being uniformly distributed according to the Galois group S_d for a given degree d > 0. Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a strengthening temperature gradient at 78 degrees latitude and displayed a hexagonal shape. This indicates that a particular type of atmospheric wave, previously thought to influence temperatures deep in the planet's atmosphere, has the ability to impact levels as high as 0.5 miles above the clouds. The dissolution of the northern vortex typically begins in the fall, but it's unclear if it will survive the winter as it did in the southern hemisphere. The discovery of the hexagonal shape of the northern vortex also sheds light on the dynamics of the middle atmosphere on the entire planet. The findings from this study are a result of the extensive data collected by the Cassini spacecraft and are a significant advancement in the understanding of Saturn's polar atmosphere and its seasonal variations. The current research is being continued by modeling the formation of the southern hemisphere's polar vortex in the months leading up to the equinox in 2009. The model suggests that the vortex may have formed more quickly than previously thought and that its formation was influenced by a particular type of atmospheric wave that varied in intensity over the course of the year. The model is also being used to investigate the differences in temperature and chemistry within the southern hemisphere's polar vortex during its summer. The results of these simulations are yet to be analyzed and will be subject to further study. The model is a starting point for a broader investigation of the formation of the polar vortices in both hemispheres and will be refined in the process. The findings from this study and the current research are a result of the collaboration between NASA, the European Space Agency, and the Cassini mission scientists. The data collected by the Cassini spacecraft is freely available to the public and has enabled a comprehensive understanding of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex in Saturn.

It is essential to note that the approach used here differs significantly from the method employed by Holmer and Roudenko, which relied on the concavity of variance to draw conclusions about solutions in an infinite domain. This informal note begins by illustrating some technical concepts, including the re-normalization of measures on orbital integrals from the works of Langlands, Frenkel-Langlands-Ng\^o, and Altug's research on Beyond Endoscopy. We discuss specific measures related to algebraic tori and explain how they relate to Tamagawa numbers. We then examine the GL2 case in depth. Additionally, the appendix by Matthew Koster clarifies the connection between the geometric measure of orbits and Kirillov's measure of co-adjoint orbits within the dual space of certain Lie algebras, including sl2 and so3.

The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract information about a sample's physical, chemical, or biological properties. In nuclear physics, x-ray scattering provides critical information about the behavior and interactions of electrons within atoms and molecules, while also offering insights into a sample's nuclear properties. This two-part work aims to introduce resonant x-ray scattering as a tool for extracting nuclear phase information and demonstrate this concept using a specific example involving the $^{24}$Mg isotope. Magnetized $^{24}$Magnetum meso-crystals are studied using RBS in search of the predicted $3p_{3/2}$ affine zero-field splitting in nuclear magnetic moments. This research provides a starting point for expanding resonant x-ray scattering's applicability to other areas, both nuclear and beyond.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Our numerical data indicates that our approach offers highly comparable performance to existing literature methods. Our proposed method is also made available through the FEniCs open-source computational platform. A notable customization of the method is shown through the application of boundary fractures. This has shown the potential for further development, such as the incorporation of multiple intersecting fractures, though it also presents several challenges. A comprehensive set of numerical examples, along with relevant Python code, can be found in the Appendix. This approach offers a significant step forward in solving real-world problems, given the common occurrence of blocking fractures in natural settings. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. Additionally, we discuss the limitations of Bayes factor analysis and potential alternatives, such as Bayesian model averaging, and leave them for future investigation. Lastly, we acknowledge the generous support of the Australian Research Council (DP160101441).

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use. This dataset can be utilized for various purposes such as validating models that generate discourse indicators, selecting the most suitable indicators for classification tasks, and developing a standardized classification system for English discourse indicators. Experimental evaluations on DiscSense demonstrate that using the predicted indicators that correspond to the underlying semantic relations in a dataset leads to a better performance compared to a random baseline, and a case study is presented to demonstrate the versatility of this dataset by extracting a subset of instances related to the "cause-effect" relation. This subset can be employed as a sample for the community of researchers working on the automatic generation of discourse indicators. The research is available at https://github.com/ASUSeNSEI/DiscSense. For any queries or feedback, please visit https://www.asu.edu/sensei.

We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. Finally, we outline the proof of our main results and discuss the relationship with an alternative geometry used in an unrelated work. This research was conducted in collaboration with Yongsheng Sheng and Song Zi Yang.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. Now, another example is given which also contests the conjecture originally presented by those authors. A bipartite graph with a girth of six and a specific degree condition cannot be colored using a particular number of colors, proving this conjecture to be false. This new example differs significantly from the previous one cited in 2021, as it utilizes a non-homogeneous vertex set. Also examined is a related conjecture proposed by Faudree and Schelp in 1990 which has now clearly been disproven. This new counterexample is then combined with another result for a large family of bipartite graphs with a girth of four to demonstrate that in such graphs, the need to use a specific number of colors can be determined on a case-by-case basis rather than relying on a general rule. Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. Following the successful use of activation clipping, we have developed a prototype to demonstrate that range control can serve as a trustworthy error detection and prevention method for classifier CNNs, specifically against common memory malfunctions in a binary floating point system. We also explore non-uniform data restriction techniques that efficiently minimize silent errors and hardware-induced data corruptions. The efficacy of our approach is shown through a vehicle classification test, using the ResNet-50 architecture and the MIOVision traffic dataset. The results provided can serve as a foundation for further research and more intricate CNN reliability cases. The code for our prototype is available online.

Additionally, we have obtained specific formulae for its associated star product and twisted coproduct. Furthermore, we have established that our generalized version is equivalent to a 1-cochain-derived twist from the basic Jordanian twist. As a result, we have both simplified and unified previously reported generalizations of the Jordanian twist. As a significant discovery, we have found that our generalized version belongs to a one-parameter family of Jordanian twists. As a proof of this finding, we have compared our generalization with the classical Jordanian twist, commonly expressed in a $r$-symmetrized format, following the guidelines of the original author. As a notable side finding, we have also obtained the one-parameter family of 1-cochain derivatives, from which the generalized version can be obtained by taking the 1-cochain equal to zero. As a significant contribution, we have also obtained the formula for the inverse of the generalized Jordanian twist. As a particular case of the one-parameter family, we have derived the formula for the twist that was previously reported by its own author.
