We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level patterns, and linguistic properties, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases like WordNet. We employ a cluster-consistent objective function to align these clusters, incorporating a novel approach to handle WordNet's hierarchical tree format. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. Our code is available at GitHub: https://github.com/ghrua/MCSE.

The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV is
reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality intervals spanning from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb
collisions based on final-state particle count. Investigating Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions 
with similar charged-particle counts allows for comparison of initial geometric 
properties and flow behaviour. Detailed comparison shows that the radial flow remains 
constant regardless of colliding system at the same multiplicity level, 
with observed particle ratio patterns holding true in medium-sized nucleus 
collisions. Also, our research reaffirms LHC energy observations of low 
proton-to-pion ratios relative to thermal models and rising $\phi$-to-pion ratios
with increased final-state particle count. Exclusive analysis of the lightest 
hadron species reveals that initial temperature and charge density are similar 
in Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions at the same multiplicity level, suggesting that
thermalisation occurs at the early stage of particle production. Concluding, our
results demonstrate early thermalisation and radial flow persistence in Xe-Xe 
collisions at the LHC. A vast range of data points is available via the J-PET 
website: https://jpet.agh.edu.pl/. A detailed paper is available at DOIs: 10.1016/j.physletb.2023.117011; 10.1016/j.physletb.2023.117012; 10.1016/j.physletb.2023.117013; 10.1016/j.physletb.2023.117014; 10.1016/j.physletb.2023.117015; 10.1016/j.physletb.2023.117016; 10.1016/j.physletb.2023.117017; 10.1016/j.physletb.2023.117018; 10.1016/j.physletb.2023.117019; 10.1016/j.physletb.2023.117020; 10.1016/j.physletb.2023.117021; 10.1016/j.physletb.

In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. This limitation is compounded by the presence of Santiago's natural barriers within the model's representation. To address this shortcoming and improve the model's ability to simulate Santiago's riots, the model needs to be modified to include a critical population displacement threshold and account for the city's natural boundaries. This proposed model successfully recreates the distribution of riots in Santiago and provides insights into the importance of population displacement and urban geography in shaping the disorders' spatial development. It also highlights the difficulties faced by authorities in regaining control over areas distant from the unrest's origin following the initial rioting. This model's limitations are, however, worth noting as it struggles to replicate the temporal progression of the riots in Santiago with the current parameters. This model's potential applications in other urban settings are also discussed. This research was conducted as part of the author's Master's degree at the University of Lyon. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of rewriting rules and normal form transformations, and a corresponding algorithm to find a containment solution using a combination of our rewriting system and the Knuth-Bendix algorithm, with an accompanying proof of its correctness. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this method with a practical example from a real-world application. The developed technique is implemented in the freeware REsolve environment for symbolic manipulation with regular expressions. The research also explores potential future developments, including the integration of transducers and weighted automata, and expands the underlying theory of regular expression solving with a generalization of the Monoid Theorem. Lastly, we examine the relationship between regular expressions and first-order logic with the successor function, demonstrating the solvability of first-order logic inequalities with the successor function in the context of non-deterministic finite transducers. The associated source code is available at the DXR repository for analysis. The underlying proofs for the developed algorithms and associated theorems are found in the appendices. Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. This paper proposes an external memory attention learning-based VIO framework, capable of efficiently combining the data from both the camera and inertial sensors for state estimation, and we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this model by accurately estimating the pose in various challenging scenarios, surpassing even the traditional and current state-of-the-art VIO baselines in various scenes. Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. Ultimately, our findings suggest that 5D bulk systems with double-honeycomb structures can serve as ideal square-root topological materials, facilitating robust mid-gap states in 3D heterostructures.

This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on an inaccessible boundary segment using data from the accessible part of a confined domain. A non-iterative approach to solving the problem is examined and different hybrid mathematical formulations are introduced. Key aspects, such as stability, convergence and smoothness of solutions are demonstrated through rigorous analysis. Edge finite elements are employed to discretize the problem. Computational results, covering two- and three-dimensional cases and accounting for noisy input data, showcase the method's effectiveness. This research was previously presented at the 2019 conference on inverse problems in Inria's annual meeting.

This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. The code for FedSA is publicly accessible at https://github.com/DeepConsortia/FedSA.

We analyze the rank growth of elliptic curves from rational numbers to quartic extensions in the Galois groups $S_4$ and $A_4$, and investigate how rank varies in different quartic fields for a fixed elliptic curve. Notably, we find an example where an elliptic curve has a rank of 13 in a $S_4$ extension, demonstrating that there are elliptic curves with arbitrarily large rank in certain number fields. Additionally, we establish the existence of an elliptic curve with a rank of 5 in a $A_4$ extension, providing a counterexample to a previous conjecture. Moreover, we examine the rank growth in both $S_4$ and $A_4$ extensions and reveal that the rank of an elliptic curve can remain 0 in certain $S_4$ extensions, given specific Diophantine conditions. These findings extend the work of Gross, Goldstein, and Kuo, as well as of Jorgenson and Lang, who investigated rank growth in cubic extensions. The research involves developing methods for controlling the rank growth of elliptic curves in quadratic extensions and extending these results to the case of $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions, as well as examining the relationship between the rank growth of an elliptic curve and the structure of its associated Galois group. The paper also includes an analysis of the rank growth in a specific $A_4$ extension where the rank of an elliptic curve can vary freely. The research further leads to the discovery of an infinite family of elliptic curves with arbitrarily large rank in a particular $S_4$ extension, and the findings are supported by a recent generalization of the Neron models over global fields of characteristic zero. The results are also validated by a recent generalization of the Shaferevich-Weil theory for abelian varieties. The research involves collaboration with G. Weng, and the papers Rank Growth of Elliptic Curves in $S_4$ and $A_4$ Quartic Extensions of the Rationals (ArXiv:2110.06330) and An Infinite Family of Elliptic Curves with Arbitrarily Large Rank in a Specific $S_4$ Extension of the Rationals (ArXiv:2207.06387). A crucial boundary, the quantum null energy condition, is used to measure the change in a region's entanglement entropy along a null direction in order to understand the quantum thermodynamics of complex systems. Investigating whether the quantum null energy condition limits irreversible entropy generation during quenching driven by an influx of energy and momentum from an infinite, memoryless bath within two-dimensional holographic theories, our research finds that an increase in both entropy and temperature, as required by the classical Clausius inequality, is necessary to prevent a violation of the quantum null energy condition, specifically in quenching transitions that result in changes in thermal states dual to Banados-Teitelboim-Zanelli geometries. Additionally, our research provides lower and upper bounds for the change in entropy or temperature for a specific change in temperature or entropy in any initial state. Our results demonstrate that the entanglement entropy within a segment of a null extended region will increase for quenching transitions that result in an increase in temperature within the same region, whereas the upper bounds suggest that this increase is systematic, as they take the form of the quadratic growth $s^2 \geq c \Delta T^2$ or the linear growth $s \geq c' \Delta T$ for all quenching transitions, as they hold for any initial state, as they are based on the invariant properties of the trace distance between the initial and final states, as they do not depend on the specific choice of the null surface or the region from which the trace distance is measured. Our findings provide a framework for understanding the relationship between the intrinsic irreversibility of quenching transitions and the inherent entropy generation as they hold for any quenching transition in any initial state. Our research involves calculating the change in entanglement entropy for a specific class of quenching transitions from a thermal state dual to a BTZ geometry. Our results demonstrate that the change in entanglement entropy directly reflects the change in temperature within the same region. Additionally, our research introduces a new quantity, the trace distance between the initial and final states, as it provides a more robust inequality that holds for any quenching transition in any initial state. Our findings show that this new quantity is equal to the change in temperature within the same region for quenching transitions from a thermal state dual to a BTZ geometry. Our results demonstrate that the null energy condition is satisfied as an equality for these specific quenching transitions. Our research involves investigating the relationship between the trace distance and the null energy

We investigate the minimal time it takes for a qubit state to evolve from an initial state into a distinguishable state under both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we develop a crucial criterion involving two asymmetry measures that ensures a state can be distinguished from its unitary evolution with a specific error probability within a certain time. This condition enables us to rank qubit states by their distinguishability time and calculate the optimal time to release a two-level system as seen in the Landau-Zener problem. For non-unitary dynamics, we compare several bounds on distinguishability time, including a novel lower bound related to the system-environment asymmetry and expressed in terms of a specific matrix norm. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between distinguishability time and other figures of merit, including the average energy, the largest eigenvalue of the density matrix, and system-environment asymmetry. For the Landau-Zener problem, we derive an analytical expression for the smallest time $t_{\text{Dif}}$ such that the final state $\rho(t_{\text{Dif}})$ differs significantly from the initial state $\rho_0$, and demonstrate that $t_{\text{Dif}} \approx 0.57\hbar\delta$ for $\Delta\ll\hbar\delta$. Lastly, we determine the optimal universal bound on $t_{\text{Dif}}$ and the corresponding universal state $\rho_{\text{univ}}$ for a qubit system. The results presented herein generalize those found in previous studies.

Consider a unit cube, $Q_n$, in $n$-dimensional space and a function space, $C(Q_n)$, consisting of continuous functions from $Q_n$ to $\mathbb{R}$. Define the norm of a function as its maximum absolute value over $Q_n$. Let $\Pi_1\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)$ be the set of polynomials of degree at most one, i.e., linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$. An interpolation projector $P$ is introduced that maps functions from $C(Q_n)$ to linear functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$, using nodes within $Q_n$. When the number of nodes is an Hadamard number, a simple algorithm yields an interpolation projector $P$ such that for any function $f\in C(Q_n)$, the norm of $Pf$ is bounded by a constant times the product of the distance from the set of nodes to the vertex of $Q_n$ and a factor that depends polynomially on the dimension $n$. If the number of nodes is not Hadamard, a different construction of $P$ is presented for the same purpose. Both projections $P$ are shown to satisfy this property for a specific class of functions, demonstrating the desired estimate on a set defined by the angles of $Q_n$ with certain specific angle measures. Additionally, the distance from the set of nodes to the edges of $Q_n$ is shown to be sufficient to obtain the desired estimate on the norm of $Pf$ for another class of functions. The generalization of these results to a hypercube in an arbitrary dimension is also discussed. The context and relevance of these results are established through a longer introduction. Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying and addressing decoherence-causing issues in quantum devices. Lastly, we examine the influence of material flaws on quantum circuits, concluding that etched silicon can pose a problem but that solutions exist, including replacing silicon with more suitable substrates like sapphire. We also explore the possibility of etched silicon being beneficial by converting it into Josephson junctions, thus transforming the very source of decoherence into a quantized component. We demonstrate the functionality of these junctions, with a 43% quantum coherence time as measured using a sequence of microwave pulses known as "folding" and a 20Qubit logical coherence time also found using the "folding" sequence. We envision a future where etched silicon, similar to etched silicon, becomes a standard material for quantum device fabrication. Ultimately, this research shows the value of terahertz near-field analysis in uncovering and addressing issues with quantum devices and highlights the versatility of etched silicon, a finding we believe will have a lasting impact in the field of quantum computing.

This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions. Despite significant research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's development, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, and discuss the need for further research to fully understand Venus's distinctive features. This study originally appeared as a chapter in the book "The Early Earth and the Building of the Planets" edited by J. Kramers, A. Eggebrecht, and H.D. Holland.

Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, obtaining results on the concentration rates of the posterior distribution. Additionally, this has implications for the convergence rates of Bayesian estimators. Another significant aspect in the study of event-data involves uncovering the graph that represents the connections and interactions between events, or the Granger connectivity graph. We have established the consistency of Bayesian methods in estimating this graph, particularly showing that the posterior distribution converges to the correct adjacency matrix, as does a Bayesian estimator based on a suitable loss function. One example of event-data that we have examined is neuronal activity data during visual stimulation. In this context, research has been conducted to compare Bayesian estimators based on different models, including the nonlinear Hawkes process and an inhomogeneous Markov chain, with results showing that the connections between neurons that follow the nonlinear Hawkes process model exhibit properties of synchronization and phase-locking that are not captured by the Markov chain model. One such finding is that the nodes of the Granger connectivity graph that represent synchronized relationships often occupy specific frequency bands, with results also showing that the properties of these nodes are more pronounced in areas of high visual processing, such as V1. One possible application of event-data analysis involves online detection of natural disasters such as floods and landslides, where the nonlinear Hawkes process model has been examined and shown to effectively learn from limited training data, particularly when the event types are uncertain. One such case study involves landslides and soil moisture levels in Kenya, with results demonstrating the model's capability to learn from limited data and predict the occurrence of events such as floods and landslides, even when the types of events are uncertain. One possible issue with point process models such as the nonlinear Hawkes process is multithreading, or the situation where multiple events occur simultaneously, as this can result in count data that contains crossings, as opposed to discrete events. One possible solution to this problem involves modifying the nonlinear Hawkes process model to account for multithreading, with results demonstrating that this model can capture the relationships between events of different types, both excitatory and inhibitory, as well as phenomena such as synchronized activity and phase-lock

As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. This component can modify the laser pulse polarization while simultaneously increasing the peak power, which has been demonstrated numerically with simulations. It shows that a high-intensity linearly polarized laser pulse can be converted to a higher-powered circularly polarized pulse. This conversion process achieves nearly complete efficiency, with about $98\%$ of the initial energy successfully converted. The required waveplate thickness was found to be inversely related to the electron density in the plasma and the strength of the magnetic field, which, for a specific plasma and field, was found to be approximately 1 cm. This type of plasma waveplate can serve a pivotal role in the effective deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems. It enables the clean extraction of a large number of protons or the acceleration of high-velocity particles in laser-plasma acceleration schemes, by preventing unwanted pulse polarization conversion that reduces the particle energy gain. The proposed plasma waveplate can be designed to operate at a specific wavelength, making this concept beneficial for laser systems with variable wavelength capabilities. This research was conducted using the PIC code EPOCH, which is suitable for simulating complex interactions involving multiple species and has access to large computational resources. This proposed plasma waveplate concept has been explored theoretically, and it is advisable to experimentally verify the predicted results with a simulation-guided approach. Re-examining the search for a nonzero electric dipole moment (EDM) form factor, $d_\tau(s)$, in $\tau^+\tau^-$ production via $e^+ e^-$ collisions between the $\tau$-pair threshold and $\sqrt{s} \sim 15$ GeV is considered. The optimal approach for sensitive $CP$-odd observables is explored, focusing on the real and imaginary parts of $C$, a dimensionless $CP$-odd observable defined as $C(s) = \frac{d \sigma(\tau^+ \to \tau^- \ell^+ \nu_\ell)/d \Omega}{d \sigma(\tau^+ \to \tau^- u \bar{u})/d \Omega}|_{\rm max}$. The expected sensitivity of BaBar and BESIII to $|C|_{\rm max}$ and $|d_\tau|_{\rm avg}$ at $\sqrt{s} = 10.58$ GeV is investigated, leading to limits on $|d_\tau|_{\rm avg}$ of $6.01 \times 10^{-20}$ $e$ cm and $4.45 \times 10^{-20}$ $e$ cm for the imaginary and real parts, respectively. We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario. Moreover, they occur naturally in the process of regular maximum likelihood decoding. The proposed method of defining the distance of a rank metric code also leads to a natural interpretation of the distance distribution for a specific class of rank metric codes. The paper concludes by investigating the specific case of Gabidulin codes, uncovering their distance distribution and revealing that the optimal packing arrangements for these codes are the same as those for the Hamming(1,n) code. The case of codes with rates greater than half is also examined and found to include those with a specific density property, which includes the previously studied case of extended Gabidulin codes. We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio 1.5 times the solar value. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling placed SN~2020jfo's mass within the 12 to 15 solar mass range. Semi-analytical modelling also suggested the presence of a substantial hydrogen envelope in SN~2020jfo's progenitor, which is unlikely for Type II supernovae with short plateau phases. This could be the first recorded Type II supernova with a hydrogen-rich envelope similar to those of M31N 1987J and SN~1970G. This finding is further supported by the presence of a prominent H-alpha plateau and a relatively narrow [Fe~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra. This distinctive combination of features has not been observed in any other SNe~II. This research was published in MNRAS dated 10 October 2023.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Furthermore, our findings indicate that models trained on selectively labeled datasets can handle real-world uncategorized documents with high levels of efficiency, surpassing the performance of traditional models trained on larger, more extensively labeled datasets. Our approach and associated tools are made available open-source, in the hopes of accelerating progress in this critical area. Our research also presents a compelling business case studies surrounding the issues and successes of document extraction. Our code can be found at https://github.com/deepmind/doc-extraction.

However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy. We discuss the implications of these findings for future LIGO and Virgo detectors, and explore possible enhancements to the network, including incorporating quasi-coherent searches and designing custom architectures. Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with resulting implications for managing public health policies in a way that balances strict measures with promoting diversity of urban encounters beyond the pandemic era. Additionally, it provides a framework for studying other changes in urban behavior, giving insights into the complex interplay between physical and social environments, in response to sudden events or natural trends. It also highlights the significance of income diversity in urban communities and offers a theoretical explanation for its decline, drawing from social identity theory and relative deprivation. Lastly, it suggests potential future research into the influence of COVID-19 on other aspects of urban diversity, including racial and ethnic diversity. This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with nonzero constant vorticity. We sought to analyze how a uniform shear flow affects weakly nonlinear, surface gravity waves through the use of Hamiltonian formulation and Hamiltonian transformation techniques. By applying these methods, we obtained a new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation describing the time-dependent evolution of the wave envelope. Our study confirms previous findings, revealing that the direction and intensity of the shear flow either strengthen or weaken the modulational instability of waves, depending on their characteristics. Our approach also facilitates a non-perturbative approach to determining the water's surface elevation, leveraging the Birkhoff normal form transformation to eliminate irrelevant triadic interactions. We validated our model against both direct numerical simulations of the full Euler equations and a comparable Dysthe equation proposed by Curtis, Carter, and Kalisch, discovering that it accurately replicates their results across various levels of vorticity. Our research reveals that the newly derived Dysthe equation is both physically and mathematically reliable, and that it can be effectively applied to study the behavior of random surface waves in a similar context. Our model's limitations are discussed, along with potential avenues for further improvement, such as accounting for boundary effects and random wave phenomena. Our results demonstrate that the newly proposed Dysthe equation can be employed to investigate the complex interactions between water waves and their surrounding environment. Our study provides a framework for other similar research, such as investigating how water waves interact with bottom topography or other elements that disrupt the flow's uniformity. The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance. Moreover, our findings highlight potential areas for improvement in recent state-of-the-art approaches relying on the BERT base model, with further analysis into the limitations and areas for future research in the field. The code for this project is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/abhishek821992/CMTR-BERT.

The study focuses on analyzing a specific aspect of these systems – the geometry of their parametric space – using statistical tools to simulate and model the systems' dynamics. The results revealed an intriguing phenomenon dubbed the "curvature effect," where a significant increase in a system's disorder is associated with an irregular geometric change, linked to the emergence of an internal timeline that influences the systems' progression over time. The findings also highlight the importance of considering a particular mathematical feature, known as "topological entropy," in modeling and understanding complex systems and their natural development. This innovative design enables efficient and scalable navigation by limiting the impact of local changes on the global map and reducing the computational requirements of mapping and inference. Experimental results, conducted using a simulated 2D environment and a real-world 3D scenario with a mobile robot, demonstrate the benefits of HiTMap: it significantly outperforms the traditional single-global-map approach in tasks involving substantial changes to the environment, and it provides a much-needed balance between mapping precision and system complexity. Furthermore, HiTMap can be integrated with hierarchical control systems for enhanced performance. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  The DynaSOAr framework is particularly well-suited for a range of real-world scientific and engineering applications, including numerical linear algebra, graph algorithms, and molecular dynamics simulations.  Our framework source code is available under the permissive BSD license and can be downloaded from https://github.com/arthurconvy/DynaSOAr.

Utilizing this framework, we examined single manganese adatoms and paired adatoms on the Nb(110) surface and compared the results to experimental findings, also deriving insights into spin-orbit coupling, magnetocrystalline anisotropy, and Kondo-like behavior. Key results include the identification of distinct YSR states corresponding to different orbital symmetries, the demonstration of how the YSR gap depends on the local magnetic field and spin-orbit coupling, and the prediction of new phenomena such as inter-atom interactions and effects of the YSR states on the host electron spectrum. Moreover, this framework is applicable to other transition metal adatoms and paired adatoms on superconducting surfaces. The theoretical predictions are compared with scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy data for a single manganese adatom and a dimer paired on the Nb(110) surface. The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate called TOI-712.05 with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By considering multiple possible orientations of the planetary systems, the team found that the four planets reside within a compact multi-planet arrangement called a mean motion resonance. Specifically, TOI-712 d, TOI-712 e, and TOI-712 f are locked in a $3:1:4$ resonance, where the time it takes each planet to complete one orbital period is in a $3$, $4$, and $1$ ratio respectively. This unique resonance likely took shape in its early stages and could have a protective effect on the inner planets' habitability. Although TOI-712 e is too large to support life, the newly discovered TOI-712 f exists within the habitable zone and has a surface temperature suitable for retaining liquid water, making it a promising exoplanet for future study. This finding adds to the limited number of detected multi-planet systems in similar resonant arrangements and provides valuable insights into the early development of the solar system and TOI-712's formation history. Further research into this system, including direct imaging and spectroscopic analysis of the exoplanetary system and TOI-712 itself, is likely to reveal more details about this fascinating system. This discovery was made possible by the $TESS$ mission and the follow-up observations with the MMT 6.5m telescope and the MEGARA optical spectrograph. This research is an exciting addition to the limited number of detected multi-planet systems in similar resonant arrangements and provides valuable insights into the early development of the solar system and TOI-712's formation history. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  Lastly, our calculations highlight the significance of accurately modeling the geometry of these defects to prevent incorrect interpretations of experimental data.  Moreover, we suggest that experimental verification of the predicted CO and NO dimer formations could yield new insights, such as the presence of positively charged oxygen ions within TiO2.  This could potentially lead to a breakthrough in fields like nuclear physics and chemistry. This could be potentially crucial information for future nanoscale experiments. This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively. The elastic potential at the Large Hadron Collider highlights the importance of the ATLAS and CMS forward proton detectors as well as the suitability of forward acceptance for searches and measurements in future colliders. The associated Monte Carlo code is made available for public use.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using higher-dimensional qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that qudits can achieve accurate results in quntum simulations of sQED for a wider range of noise intensities compared to their qubit-based counterparts. Moreover, when comparing the efficiency of different qudit sizes, our results indicate that higher-dimensional qudits systematically offer greater tolerance to noise, as seen in our calculations of threshold noise intensities for both noise types. To achieve these findings, we utilized a variational approach with the most compact qudit eigenshades collection, identifying that the optimal qudit size varies with the level of noise. Specifically, our analysis showed that qudits of dimensionality d=7 are particularly suitable for examining the mass gap in sQED simulations. Our research suggests that developing noise-reducing protocols tailored to target physical quantities, rather than generic qudit dimensions, may lead to even more significant noise tolerance improvements. Ultimately, our analysis implies that in $(1+1)$d sQED, it's feasible to operate well beyond the threshold for amplitude damping noise, but in $(1+1)$d sQED, it's only possible to operate below a certain level of Pauli channel noise. To further facilitate this research, we have made our qudits noise tolerance data available online. Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations accounting for the polarization of both electrons and positrons and reveals that positrons produced when a high-intensity laser interacts with a dense, elongated target may harbor significant polarization properties. In fact, the polarization of the positrons could reach 30% or more, accompanied by a dense positron cloud with high polarization, exceeding 10% in certain cases. This phenomenon is particularly observable with petawatt-class lasers and may be studied at facilities like the Apollo project or similar setups. If successfully harnessed, this feature has the potential to greatly enhance the utility of positrons produced in such experiments.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup of a particular size that is both normal and has a substantial number of conjugate elements within it. This result reinforces an earlier finding by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes. Additionally, it establishes a connection between these groups and those with a large generating rank, which includes groups with a prime order and certain nilpotent groups. A computational example for a symmetric group is also provided. This work was previously published in a paper titled Finite groups with a polynomial diameter.

This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C. A corresponding digital backend was designed to meet the 2.4MHz frequency detection rate requirement, and it was successfully integrated into a 180nm CMOS process with a minimal silicon area of 0.153$mm^2$. A comprehensive analysis of recently published temperature sensors demonstrated that the proposed design excels in various key performance metrics. A simple yet efficient digital backend was also developed to facilitate the measurement of thermal gradients and time-domain temperatures. The corresponding test chip, which features a 5mm$^2$ silicon area, was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, and it yielded accurate results in two different scenarios. The design of the temperature sensor and the digital backend is highly versatile, and it can be employed in a wide range of applications, including automotive, aerospace, and industrial systems that require precise thermal monitoring, adaptive voltage and frequency scaling, and robust safety and security protocols. This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric constructs over Lie groupoids and differential stacks. Building on the foundations laid out in [arXiv:2103.04560, arXiv:2012.08447, arXiv:2012.08442, arXiv:1907.00375], the study establishes connections between key concepts within the field. Notably, a significant correlation between gerbes over stacks has been established in [arXiv:1907.00375], the relationship between the sheaf-theoretic definition of gerbes and the approach based on geometric objects along surfaces was examined in [arXiv:2012.08447], the equivalence between the categorification of the fundamental group using the complex $K(\pi,1)$ and the classifying space $B\pi$ was explored in [arXiv:2012.08442], and the development of the Chern-Weil transform was introduced in [arXiv:2103.04560]. A key contribution of this research is the discovery that the sheaf-theoretic definition of gerbes can be translated into the language of geometric objects along surfaces, along with the proof that the fundamental group of a stack is isomorphic to the group of loops around that stack. Moreover, a transformation was established that maps gerbes from one stack to the geometric objects along surfaces, resulting in the development of a connection without flat part. Finally, the research examines the application of this connection to define cohomology classes using the Chern-Weil transform, along with the examination of a specific example related to the Riemann surface $\mathbb{H}/\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$. A significant outcome of this research is the discovery that the space of sections for the gerbe over the stack $\mathrm{Bun}_G(\mathrm{C}^{\mathrm{an}})$ is given by the algebra of regular functions over the affine space with coordinates given by the Markov numbers, along with the finding that the cohomology classes associated with the Riemann surface $\mathbb{H}/\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ can be represented as polynomials in the Weyl chamber weights. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  It's also crucial to investigate the timescales and core growth pathways that may lead to massive star formation, given that not all cores will eventually form massive protostars.  It's possible that all cores, regardless of their mass, have an equal chance of forming a massive protostar, given the right environmental conditions.  This discovery's significance extends beyond the Dragon cloud, as it may describe a universal pathway for massive star formation that's independent of specific environments.  It's conceivable that a similar core growth process that starts with starless cores of any mass could account for the massive star formation observed in other molecular clouds.  High dynamic range surveys for both prestellar and protostellar objects are necessary to test this hypothesis fully.  It's also vital to develop a core and star formation mass function, as it may provide insights into the core and star formation mass functions' origin, formation, and evolution. Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness. The application of these operators to the expansion of zonal functions on the sphere leads to one-step recurrence formulas. The paper also explores the relationship between these recurrences and the previous results concerning the differentiation and integration methods used on the sphere. Additionally, it provides a strict positive definite example that cannot be generated using the previously introduced methods. The paper concludes by discussing the implications and potential uses of these new one-step recurrence formulas in various contexts. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We identified three distinct modes of flow: surface motion alone, surface and inner shell interaction, and deep shell interaction depending on the degree of surface roughness. By correlating stress data with visual observations, we established a framework that explains how surface roughness impacts friction forces and inner shell behavior. Furthermore, we propose a simplified model to demonstrate how surface roughness influences the curvature of the inner shells and propose that the minimum inner shell curvature necessary for stable shell interaction could be a critical parameter in this context. This parameter, however, would benefit from further validation through additional experiments. Nonetheless, our current findings suggest that surface roughness can be an important factor in determining the resistance liquids and foams encounter during flow. This knowledge can be used to better understand a variety of phenomena including river flooding, foam lamination, and the flow of pasty liquids. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. Code is available at GitHub: https://github.com/ghrua/LAANMT.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. In the process, we highlight valuable insights that can be applied to other projects in the field of translational computer science. A translational perspective is also beneficial for understanding the relationship between grid computing concepts and implementations. This connection is reflected in the alignment between the Open Grid Services Architecture and the Globus Toolkit layers. In the course of our analysis, we identify additional insights relevant to the fields of service-oriented architecture and cloud computing. These insights pertain to the challenges of moving from abstract designs to practical implementations and the importance of considering issues like security, reliability, and ease of use when defining these architectures. Ultimately, our exploration demonstrates the benefits of a translational perspective for understanding the development of grid computing and identifies opportunities for further research into the interplay between design and implementation in other complex systems. A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation, which yields results when plotted against a set of current Hubble data. Our analysis of the model reveals that despite its quintessence-like nature, it surpasses the phantom barrier. To assess the model's predictions for the universe's evolution, we investigate the development of the deceleration parameter, the cosmic density, and the effective equation of state parameter for both the model and its embedded dark energy component. Our findings also support a value of 8 × 10^6 Pa.s for the model's current-day viscosity coefficient, which corroborates several past studies. This model predicts that the universe will return to a dust-like state in its remote future, and it also accounts for the observed acceleration and the underlying viscosity of the cosmic fluid. Our analysis of the model's parameters reveals that its current attractor solution occurs at densities below the critical density of the current universe. This model's ability to account for the observed galaxy velocity curvature disposes of any necessity to include its inherent graininess when analyzing the Hubble length scale. This model's future predictions can be verified through future observations of the Hubble constant at high redshifts. This unified dark fluid model also provides a potential explanation for the universe's current high-degree viscosity. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude. For example, for a dipole dark sector, this facility could lower the limit from 100 GeV to as low as 10 MeV, thereby exploring a previously unexplored region of the parameter space. We have made the code for these analyses publicly available. The findings of this research hold significance for theories such as the dark photon, the neutrino dipole, and the littlest Higgs with T-Parity. The effective field theories used in this analysis provide a clear path for interpreting J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter and offer insights that can be applied to similar processes in other charmonium states or electron scattering off nucleons. The code for these analyses is available at https://github.com/chenhengxian/JPsiAnalysis. The findings of this research have been presented at the 2022 Lepton Photon Conference. This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. Moreover, this methodology allows researchers to develop custom-trained models for a variety of biomedical applications, including kidney detection in CT scans, tumor detection in MRI scans, and more. Experimental evaluations conducted on datasets related to liver biopsy and kidney biopsy revealed that the proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of both performance metrics. To this end, for two given irreducible admissible generic representations of G, with shared central character and gamma factors, our result stipulates that these representations are isomorphic. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, revealing that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. A numerical experiment demonstrates the effectiveness of GCNNs in learning from small datasets, showcasing the matched filtering interpretation in action. A discussion on the limitations and future extensions of the GCNN framework is also provided. A new concept called the Spectral Residual GCNN is introduced as an analytical approach to better understand GCNNs, revealing that the information learned in earlier layers primarily relates to the input data structure rather than providing sufficient representation for downstream classification tasks, which can be addressed by the SR-GCNN. A numerical experiment on real datasets shows that the SR-GCNN outperforms the traditional GCNN. The matched filtering interpretation of GCNNs provides valuable insights into designing more effective and data structure aware GCNNs. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Moreover, the findings demonstrate a notable 2.5 dB improvement in the signal-to-noise ratio of the estimated mechanical properties. The proposed method has the potential to broaden the VSSA imaging technique's applications in elastography. Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we examine the behavior of weak bosons both in isolation (in the WPM approximation) and in combination with QCD, exploring both narrow and broad resonance phenomena. Moreover, we demonstrate how the Effective Vector Boson Approximation (EVBA) enhances the accuracy of physical predictions, particularly in the regime where the scattering process involves multiple weak bosons. The EVBA approach proves particularly beneficial for facilitating rapid cross-section calculations, despite the involvement of complex strong and electroweak interactions. The introduction of EVBA enables a significant boost in the energy range that can be effectively explored with a muon collider, extending upwards of 30 TeV, and we outline the key outcomes of our calculations. The Effective Vector Boson Approximation is an enhancement to existing programs, as demonstrated by comparing cross-section calculations for a single weak boson resonances produced in muon-muon collisions within the EVBA and WPM contexts, yielding differences of no more than several percent. The EVBA is also an adaptable framework, as shown by the minimal impact it has on the distribution patterns of the scattered particles. The inclusion of EVBA is particularly advantageous for improving the accuracy of predictions for multi-weak boson scattering processes, and we present calculations for three weak boson scattering scenarios in both isolated and combined contexts, in addition to outlining feasible detection pathways for these processes with a muon collider. The inclusion of EVBA effectively broadens the range of energy levels that can be efficiently investigated with a muon collider, as illustrated by the inclusion of the $WWZ$ and $WW/\gamma$ processes that become accessible above 14/10 TeV, and the inclusion of the $WWW$ process that becomes accessible above 20 TeV, and we discuss the technical requirements for achieving this expanded range of capabilities with a muon collider. benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using

performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our results demonstrate that both model-based multi-task reinforcement
learning with isolated dynamics networks and a related policy approach, which
utilizes a single shared model, exhibit superior performance compared to using a
single learned dynamics model. Moreover, we observe that our proposed approach
excels in reducing catastrophic interference between tasks. Our code is publicly

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. Moreover, our method's ability to produce high-quality samples permits the derivation of important metrics like the posterior distribution's entropy and the mean posterior density ratio, which are crucial in determining whether prior and posterior distributions differ or not, and whether certain image restoration or reconstruction problems have a single unique solution or multiple probable outcomes. We open-sourced our code and data generated during the study are available at https://github.com/alvinenan/CGAN-posterior.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. This finding is supported by previous studies that defined the boundaries of the Local Bubble based on the distance to isolated hot white dwarfs and the presence of a localized void in the 21 cm all-sky map of neutral hydrogen. This discovery demonstrates the capability of pulsar scintillation to detect and analyze the properties of screens in the local interstellar medium, providing insights into the anatomy of the Local Bubble. The velocity of the screen also appears turbulent, with variations on both large and small scales, which may help explain the origins of the Local Bubble's shape and size. The data and analysis are available online for further investigation. The approach to analyzing scintillation patterns and the properties of screens in the line of sight to the pulsar have applications to future observations of the pulsar with higher sensitivity equipment. The association of this screen with the Local Bubble offers a unique opportunity to study the properties of the bubble and its boundaries in the solar neighborhood. The findings from this analysis highlight the value of long-term pulsar scintillation observations and the potential of future surveys for detecting screens associated with the local interstellar medium.
